exams.title: Practice Test 1

qs.q:
Dear Sir or Madam,
a. It overheats when I play games and it keeps crashing when I do my homework. It also sometimes slows down when I watch movies.
b. Finally, I spoke to your colleague, Andy. He said he would speak to his manager and call back in ten minutes. That was three hours ago.
c. On Friday, November 27th, I bought a Link76 laptop from your website and it is not working. The laptop has two main problems.
d. I called RocketTech's customer hotline and waited 30 minutes to speak to someone.
e. I would like RocketTech to repair my laptop or provide a new one as soon as possible. I look forward to your reply.
Yours faithfully,
June Evans
qs.ex:
**Vì sao đáp án A (c - a - d - b - e) đúng:**

Thư khiếu nại có trình tự logic như sau:
- **c**: Mở đầu, nêu thời điểm mua hàng và nói chung "two main problems".
- **a**: Mô tả cụ thể hai vấn đề (quá nóng, treo máy), nối tiếp trực tiếp câu "two main problems".
- **d**: Kể lại hành động đã làm: gọi hotline, chờ 30 phút.
- **b**: "Finally, I spoke to... Andy" tiếp nối d, và "Finally" báo hiệu kết quả của quá trình gọi điện.
- **e**: Kết thư bằng yêu cầu giải quyết, đi cùng "I look forward to your reply".

**Cần chú ý các đáp án còn lại:**
- **B, C**: Đặt d ngay sau c, làm đứt mạch vì "two main problems" cần được giải thích ngay bằng a.
- **C, D**: Đặt e trước b, sai vì lời yêu cầu phải là phần kết thư. Ngoài ra "Finally" trong b không thể đứng sau phần kết.

Lưu ý: hãy dựa vào từ nối và đại từ ("two problems", "Finally") để xác định thứ tự.

qs.q:
Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoặc văn bản hoàn chỉnh:
a. **Lan**: OK, Mum. I'll be home before 10 p.m. then.
b. **Lan's mother**: Certainly. Whose birthday is it?
c. **Lan**: Mum, can I go to my friend's birthday party this Saturday evening?
d. **Lan's mother**: Oh, I'm afraid not. You must come back home before 10 p.m. We're going to visit your grandparents early on Sunday morning.
e. **Lan**: It's Mai's birthday, Mum. Is it OK if I stay the night at her house after the party?
qs.ex: Đáp án C (c-b-e-d-a): Lan xin phép đi dự tiệc (c); mẹ đồng ý và hỏi sinh nhật ai (b); Lan trả lời và xin ngủ lại (e); mẹ từ chối, giải thích lý do (d); Lan chấp nhận (a). Cấu trúc: Can I...? / Is it OK if...? xin phép; I'm afraid not từ chối lịch sự.

qs.q:
Dear Mr. Hoa An,
a. I am writing to express my interest in the position of teaching assistant at Better-You Language Centre.
b. I took my IELTS test three months ago and got an overall score of 8.0.
c. I am currently in grade 12 at Le Hong Phong High School for the Gifted and I am looking for a part-time job.
d. I also have previous experience of working as a volunteer at SOS Children's Village in Ho Chi Minh City.
e. I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss the position further.
Yours sincerely,
qs.ex: Đáp án B (a-c-b-d-e): (a) mở đầu nêu mục đích viết thư; (c) giới thiệu bản thân và lý do tìm việc; (b) đưa bằng chứng năng lực (IELTS 8.0); (d) bổ sung kinh nghiệm bằng 'also'; (e) kết thư bày tỏ mong muốn được trao đổi thêm. Đây là cấu trúc thư xin việc chuẩn.

qs.q:
Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoặc văn bản hoàn chỉnh:
a. **Sam**: I was thinking about the exam next week. I'm a bit nervous about it, to be honest.
b. **Ann**: Oh, hi, Sam! How are you?
c. **Ann**: So am I. But you? I'm surprised at that. I thought you studied a lot.
qs.ex: Đáp án B (b - a - c): Hội thoại bắt đầu bằng lời chào và hỏi thăm của Ann (b: 'Oh, hi, Sam! How are you?'). Sam trả lời và nói mình lo lắng về kỳ thi (a). Ann đáp lại 'So am I' (c), cấu trúc đồng tình 'So + trợ động từ/be + chủ ngữ', nên c phải đứng sau a.

qs.q:
Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoặc văn bản hoàn chỉnh:
a. Secondly, there need to be more police in the area preventing people from cutting down trees. A lot of the people who cut them down do it illegally. If they were more afraid of getting caught, they might stop.
b. First of all, we have to make the local people aware of the damage they're doing.
c. Every day, thousands and thousands of trees are cut down in the Amazonian rainforest.
d. It's a very serious problem, and there's no easy solution, but we're short of time. It won't be long before the rainforests disappear completely.
e. This does enormous damage to the local environment, and also possibly affects the world's climate. But how can we save the rainforests from destruction?
qs.ex: Đáp án B: c - e - b - a - d. Câu c mở đầu nêu hiện tượng chặt cây hằng ngày. Câu e có 'This' chỉ hậu quả của c và đặt câu hỏi cách cứu rừng. Câu b 'First of all' nêu giải pháp thứ nhất, a 'Secondly' nêu giải pháp thứ hai, d kết luận về tính cấp bách.

qs.p:
Smart Ways to Save Money – Start Small, Think Big!
Many people think that saving money is difficult, but with a few small habits, you can (6) ____________ simple tasks that make a big difference.
Start by tracking your daily spending. You might be shocked to see (7) ____________ of money you spend on utilities each month.
Cutting out small, unnecessary (8) ____________ each day can lead to significant savings over time.
Another tip is to use budgeting apps or tools to help manage your finances. These can provide helpful (9) ____________ into your spending habits and show you where to cut back.
Finally, many buyers tend to ignore price comparisons before making a big purchase. (10) ____________, taking the time to compare prices carefully can help you find a better deal and save (11) ____________ money in the long run.
qs.q: Chỗ trống (6)
qs.ex: Carry out nghĩa là thực hiện, tiến hành; hợp với 'simple tasks' (những việc đơn giản). Cut down là cắt giảm, bring over là mang đến, put up là dựng lên hoặc tăng giá, đều không hợp nghĩa. Cấu trúc: carry out + tasks.

qs.p:
Smart Ways to Save Money – Start Small, Think Big!
Many people think that saving money is difficult, but with a few small habits, you can (6) ____________ simple tasks that make a big difference.
Start by tracking your daily spending. You might be shocked to see (7) ____________ of money you spend on utilities each month.
Cutting out small, unnecessary (8) ____________ each day can lead to significant savings over time.
Another tip is to use budgeting apps or tools to help manage your finances. These can provide helpful (9) ____________ into your spending habits and show you where to cut back.
Finally, many buyers tend to ignore price comparisons before making a big purchase. (10) ____________, taking the time to compare prices carefully can help you find a better deal and save (11) ____________ money in the long run.
qs.q: Chỗ trống (7)
qs.ex: 'the amount of money' cần cụm chỉ lượng đi với danh từ không đếm được. 'a great deal of' + danh từ không đếm được là đúng. 'a wide range of' và 'a large number of' đi với danh từ đếm được số nhiều.

qs.p:

Finally, many buyers tend to ignore price comparisons before making a big purchase. (10) ____________, taking the time to compare prices carefully can help you find a better deal and save (11) ____________ money in the long run.
qs.q: Chỗ trống (8)
qs.ex: 'expenses' là các khoản chi tiêu, thường ngày, phù hợp với 'cutting out small, unnecessary expenses' (cắt giảm chi tiêu nhỏ không cần thiết). 'Revenues' là doanh thu nên sai nghĩa; 'outlays' và 'payments' không là kết hợp từ tự nhiên ở đây.

qs.q: Chỗ trống (9)
qs.ex: 'provide insights into' là cụm cố định, nghĩa là giúp hiểu sâu về điều gì, ở đây là thói quen chi tiêu. Meanings, advances, instructions không đi với 'into your spending habits' một cách tự nhiên.

qs.q: Chỗ trống (10)
qs.ex: Câu trước nói nhiều người bỏ qua việc so sánh giá, câu sau nói nên so sánh giá: hai ý đối lập, nên dùng 'However' (tuy nhiên). Consequently và Therefore chỉ kết quả; Otherwise nghĩa là nếu không thì, không hợp ngữ cảnh.

qs.q: Chỗ trống (11)
qs.ex: 'money' là danh từ không đếm được, nên dùng 'some' (một ít). 'Few' và 'many' đi với danh từ đếm được số nhiều. 'Any' thường dùng trong câu phủ định hoặc nghi vấn, không hợp câu khẳng định này.

qs.p:
Do you enjoy cooking? Would you like to turn your passion into a profession? At KitchenCraft Academy, we offer a wide range of courses to help you become a (12) ____________ chef - from basic knife skills to advanced international cuisine.
Our tutors, (13) ____________ in Michelin-starred restaurants, will guide you every step of the way. You'll also (14) ____________ real progress in the kitchen and take part in workshops designed to inspire creativity and boost confidence.
The academy is located in the heart of the city, close (15) ____________ public transport and local markets - the perfect place (16) ____________ fresh ingredients and local flavors.
At KitchenCraft, we believe in hands-on learning and (17) ____________ to help your culinary career truly take off!
qs.q: Chỗ trống (12)
qs.ex: Sau mạo từ 'a' và trước danh từ 'chef' cần một tính từ. 'successful' (thành công) phù hợp nghĩa. 'successive' nghĩa là liên tiếp, không hợp ngữ cảnh; 'succeed' là động từ, 'successfully' là trạng từ.

qs.p:
Do you enjoy cooking? Would you like to turn your passion into a profession? At KitchenCraft Academy, we offer a wide range of courses to help you become a (12) ____________ chef - from basic knife skills to advanced international cuisine.
Our tutors, (13) ____________ in Michelin-starred restaurants, will guide you every step of the way. You'll also (14) ____________ real progress in the kitchen and take part in workshops designed to inspire creativity and boost confidence.
The academy is located in the heart of the city, close (15) ____________ public transport and local markets - the perfect place (16) ____________ fresh ingredients and local flavors.
At KitchenCraft, we believe in hands-on learning and (17) ____________ to help your culinary career truly take off!
qs.q: Chỗ trống (13)
qs.ex: Rút gọn mệnh đề quan hệ chủ động: 'who have worked/worked' thành V-ing. 'Tutors working in Michelin-starred restaurants' nghĩa là các giáo viên đang/từng làm việc ở nhà hàng sao Michelin. Chủ động nên không dùng 'worked' (bị động).

qs.p:
Do you enjoy cooking? Would you like to turn your passion into a profession? At KitchenCraft Academy, we offer a wide range of courses to help you become a (12) ____________ chef - from basic knife skills to advanced international cuisine.
Our tutors, (13) ____________ in Michelin-starred restaurants, will guide you every step of the way. You'll also (14) ____________ real progress in the kitchen and take part in workshops designed to inspire creativity and boost confidence.

At KitchenCraft, we believe in hands-on learning and (17) ____________ to help your culinary career truly take off!
qs.q: Chỗ trống (14)
qs.ex: Collocation: 'make progress' nghĩa là tiến bộ. Các động từ 'do, take, put' không đi với 'progress' theo nghĩa này. Cấu trúc: make + progress (in something).

qs.q: Chỗ trống (15)
qs.ex: Cụm 'close to + danh từ' nghĩa là gần với. Vậy 'close to public transport and local markets' (gần phương tiện công cộng và chợ địa phương). Các giới từ in, of, with không đi với 'close' trong nghĩa này.

qs.p:
[**I**] This technology overlays virtual objects and information onto real-world environments, creating interactive experiences that were once unimaginable. [**II**] AR is making waves in education, gaming, and even social interactions, promising a future where technology feels more integrated into our daily lives. [**III**] Very soon, AR could revolutionize every aspect of how we interact, with information and entertainment, making the virtual world seem as real as the one around us. [**IV**]
In education, AR is proving to be a powerful tool for engagement and understanding. Students can now explore a 3D model of the solar system in their classrooms or dissect a virtual frog without harming a real one. These experiences bring lessons to life, making complex topics easier to grasp. AR also **fosters** creativity, encouraging students to think outside the box and engage with their studies in new ways. With AR, learning is no longer confined to textbooks and lectures. **It** allows students to start strong and immediately apply what they learn, helping them dive into real-world scenarios with ease.
The entertainment industry is another area which AR has a significant impact on. Games like Pokémon Go have shown how AR can create immersive, real-world experiences that capture the imagination of millions. In the future, AR could revolutionize how we watch movies, attend concerts, or even try on clothes while shopping online. Imagine sitting in your living room and having a holographic performance appear right before your eyes. AR can also **break the mold**, introducing groundbreaking ways to entertain audiences and keep them engaged like never before. The possibilities are endless.
<u>AR is truly a golden opportunity to reshape our interaction with the world</u>. However, like any new technology, it comes with challenges. Developers and educators must ensure that AR is accessible, user-friendly, and free from misuse. With thoughtful innovation, AR has the potential to become a game-changer in both education and entertainment, bridging the gap between imagination and reality.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
Augmented reality (AR) is transforming the way we learn, work, and play by blending digital content with the physical world.
qs.ex: Câu cho sẵn giới thiệu khái niệm AR và viết đầy đủ "Augmented reality (AR)", nên phải đặt đầu đoạn, vị trí [I]. Câu kế tiếp dùng "This technology" để nhắc lại AR, còn "AR" ở câu sau đã là viết tắt. Đây là quy tắc: định nghĩa trước, thông tin chi tiết sau.

qs.q: Which of the following could best replace the phrase "**break the mold**" in paragraph 3?
qs.ex: "Break the mold" nghĩa là phá vỡ khuôn mẫu, làm điều mới mẻ, khác biệt. Vì vậy "innovate" (đổi mới, sáng tạo) là từ thay thế phù hợp nhất. Các từ maintain, copy, conserve đều mang nghĩa giữ nguyên hoặc bắt chước, trái nghĩa.

qs.p:
Apple’s iPhone 17 has quickly attracted worldwide attention. At first glance, its design may look familiar, but the phone is slimmer, lighter, and built with more recycled materials. Apple presents this as evidence of its commitment to sustainability, showing how the company responds to consumer concerns about the environment.
The new device also introduces stronger artificial intelligence features. These include instant translation, smarter photo organization, and predictive text that adapts to each user’s style. Apple **stresses** that most processing is done on the phone itself to protect privacy. Supporters welcome these tools as practical and time-saving, while critics question how much control users truly have over their data.
Battery performance has seen a clear improvement. Thanks to a redesigned cooling system, the iPhone 17 operates more efficiently and lasts nearly 20 percent longer than the iPhone 16. Reviewers, especially gamers and professionals, praise this change because **it** reduces overheating and extends daily use. Combined with faster wireless charging, the upgrade shows Apple’s attempt to answer long-standing customer complaints.
Security has also advanced with a dual biometric system combining facial recognition and voice authentication. **Apple describes this as a stronger barrier against identity theft**. Some users worry it may be difficult to set up or fail in noisy places. Even with such **doubts**, initial sales have been strong in more than 40 countries, particularly in Asia. This suggests that Apple’s effort to combine innovation, sustainability, and safety is gaining wide acceptance in the global market.
(Adapted from The Verge 2025)
qs.q: Which of the following is **NOT** mentioned as an AI feature of the iPhone 17?
qs.ex: Đoạn 2 chỉ nêu instant translation, smarter photo organization và predictive text. Video streaming không được nhắc đến nên là đáp án NOT mentioned. Kỹ năng: đối chiếu từng lựa chọn với bài, loại các ý có trong văn bản.

In the past, many Vietnamese families followed a clear rule: the mother cooked and cleaned, and the father earned money. Today, this picture is changing quickly.
A recent survey of 500 **urban** families showed interesting results. About 60 percent of the mothers had full-time jobs outside the home. Because of this, housework could no longer be only their responsibility. In 7 out of 10 families, the husband helped with cooking or cleaning at least three times a week.
Children also play an important part. In the survey, teenagers aged 15 to 17 spent an average of five hours a week on chores. **They** usually washed the dishes, swept the floor or looked after younger brothers and sisters. One student, Lan, said, "I cook dinner every Wednesday. At first I burned the rice, but now my parents love my fried fish."
Sharing chores brings many **benefits**. First, parents have more free time to rest. Second, children learn useful life skills, such as managing time and working in a team. Finally, family members understand and respect each other more.
Of course, sharing work is not always easy. Some families still argue about who does more. Experts suggest holding a short family meeting each week. Everyone can talk about what they can do and agree on a fair plan. With a little patience, housework can become a chance to bond, not a reason to fight.

qs.p:
Every family has its own traditions. These habits may seem small, but they make family members feel close and proud of who they are.
In Viet Nam, many families gather for a big meal on Tet, the Lunar New Year. Grandparents give lucky money to the children, and everyone wears new clothes. Some families also visit the graves of their **ancestors** a few days before Tet to show respect.
In Japan, families often take a New Year trip to a temple. **They** pray for health and happiness, and then they enjoy a special meal called osechi. In Mexico, a girl's fifteenth birthday is celebrated with a large party called a quinceañera. Relatives and friends dance, eat and give her gifts.
Traditions do not have to be old or famous. A survey of 1,000 families in Britain found that 40 percent had a weekly "pizza night", and 25 percent read a bedtime story to their children every day. One father said, "It takes only twenty minutes, but my daughter remembers every story."
Traditions are important for several reasons. They give children a sense of belonging. They also help different generations talk to each other. If your family does not have a tradition yet, why not start one? You could cook breakfast together every Sunday or take a walk after dinner. In time, this simple habit may become a **precious** memory.

qs.p:
As cities grow, **they** face **pressure** on roads, water, energy and housing. Fortunately, many places are using technology to make urban life easier. These ideas are often called smart city solutions.
One important area is transport. In Singapore, electronic road pricing charges drivers more when roads are busy, which encourages people to travel at different times or take public transport. In Seoul, buses and trains share one payment card, so passengers can change vehicles easily and cheaply.
Another solution is saving energy. Many cities now replace old street lamps with LED lights that use up to 50 percent less electricity. Some lights even turn on only when they detect people or cars. This reduces both costs and pollution.
Waste management is also improving. In Copenhagen, a large power plant burns household waste to produce heat and electricity for thousands of homes. Its roof has even been designed as a place for walking and skiing, showing that industry and **leisure** can exist together.
Finally, citizens play a key role. Mobile apps allow residents to report broken roads, check air quality or find free parking spaces. When people take part, cities respond faster to real needs.
Smart technology cannot solve every problem, but it gives cities useful tools for becoming cleaner, safer and more liveable.

Urbanisation is the process in which more and more people leave the countryside and **settle** in towns and cities. It is happening all over the world, and Viet Nam is no exception. According to the United Nations, more than half of the world's population now lives in urban areas, and this figure may reach about 68 percent by 2050.
One main reason for urbanisation is the search for jobs. Factories, offices and service companies are usually located in cities, so **they** offer many more opportunities than farming villages. For example, thousands of young people from the Mekong Delta move to Ho Chi Minh City every year to work in industry or open small businesses.
Education and healthcare are also important attractions. Big cities often have better universities, modern hospitals and a wider choice of schools. Many parents move to the city so that their children can have a brighter future. In addition, urban life offers entertainment, shopping centres and public transport, which make daily life more **convenient**.
However, rapid urbanisation brings serious challenges. Housing becomes expensive, and some migrants have to live in small, crowded rooms. Traffic congestion grows worse, and air pollution can harm people's health. In Ha Noi, for instance, the number of motorbikes and cars has increased sharply, causing heavy traffic at rush hour.
To deal with these problems, city governments are building new metro lines, planting more trees and developing satellite towns. If planned carefully, urbanisation can bring growth and a better quality of life for everyone.

qs.p:
As cities grow larger, planners around the world are looking for clever ways to make urban life easier and more sustainable. One popular idea is the smart city, a city that uses technology to improve services and save resources.
Transport is a good example. In Singapore, electronic road pricing charges drivers more when roads are busy, so fewer people drive at peak times. Meanwhile, mobile apps help passengers check bus and train times in **real time**. In Viet Nam, cities such as Da Nang are testing digital systems that allow residents to pay bills and send requests to local authorities online.
Green spaces are equally important. Parks and trees reduce heat, **absorb** dust and give people places to relax. Some cities have even built "vertical gardens" on the walls of tall buildings. In Seoul, an old highway was turned into a 6-kilometre stream and park, **which** now attracts thousands of visitors every day.
Waste management is another priority. Many cities encourage residents to sort rubbish at home so that plastic, paper and glass can be recycled. Some also use solar energy to power street lights, which cuts electricity costs and lowers emissions.
Of course, building a smart and green city needs money, planning and cooperation. Governments cannot do everything alone. Citizens must also play their part by saving energy, using public transport and respecting public spaces. When everyone works together, cities can become healthier, safer and more pleasant places to live.

Meanwhile, mobile apps help passengers check bus and train times in **real time**. In Viet Nam, cities such as Da Nang are testing digital systems that allow residents to pay bills and send requests to local authorities online.
Green spaces are equally important. Parks and trees reduce heat, **absorb** dust and give people places to relax. Some cities have even built "vertical gardens" on the walls of tall buildings. In Seoul, an old highway was turned into a 6-kilometre stream and park, **which** now attracts thousands of visitors every day.
Waste management is another priority. Many cities encourage residents to sort rubbish at home so that plastic, paper and glass can be recycled. Some also use solar energy to power street lights, which cuts electricity costs and lowers emissions.
Of course, building a smart and green city needs money, planning and cooperation. Governments cannot do everything alone. Citizens must also play their part by saving energy, using public transport and respecting public spaces. When everyone works together, cities can become healthier, safer and more pleasant places to live.

qs.q:
Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. A: That's amazing! How did she manage to make such a discovery with so little equipment?
b. A: Her story really shows that we must persevere when things get difficult.
c. A: Have you read about Marie Curie's groundbreaking work on radioactivity?
d. B: She spent years in a small laboratory, and her determination never weakened.
e. B: Yes, I have. She was a pioneer who won two Nobel Prizes in different sciences.
qs.ex:
**Vì sao đáp án A (c – e – a – d – b) đúng:**

Câu c là lời mở đầu hội thoại: A hỏi "Have you read about Marie Curie's...?". Câu e đáp lại trực tiếp bằng "Yes, I have", rồi giới thiệu bà là người tiên phong đạt hai giải Nobel. Câu a là phản ứng của A ("That's amazing!") và hỏi bà làm được điều đó bằng cách nào với ít thiết bị như vậy. Câu d là câu trả lời của B cho câu hỏi "How did she manage...?". Câu b kết luận bằng bài học về sự kiên trì.

**Lưu ý các đáp án còn lại:**

- B: đặt d trước a, nên câu trả lời xuất hiện trước câu hỏi.
- C: đặt a lên đầu, nhưng "That's amazing!" chưa có thông tin nào để phản ứng.
- D: đặt a ngay sau c, làm "Yes, I have" của e mất câu hỏi để đáp lại.

Học sinh cần chú ý cặp hỏi – đáp và các từ phản hồi như "Yes, I have", "That's amazing!".

qs.q:
Dear Linh,
a. His contribution shows how careful observation can change the world.
b. In 1928, he noticed that mold in his laboratory had killed the bacteria around it.
c. Please tell me when you are free, and we can watch it together. Best wishes, Minh
d. I have just finished a documentary about Alexander Fleming, and I think you would enjoy it.
e. This accidental discovery became a breakthrough that led to penicillin and saved millions of lives.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. A: I see. So imagination was as important as equipment for him.
b. A: Did he do many experiments to prove them?
c. A: Which scientist do you admire most, Nam?
d. B: Not really. He mostly used thought experiments and mathematics, and other scientists tested his ideas later.
e. B: Albert Einstein, because his innovative ideas changed how we see time and space.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. Using X-ray technology, she produced a clear image known as Photo 51.
b. However, her work was not widely recognised during her lifetime.
c. Today, she is remembered as a talented scientist of modern biology.
d. Rosalind Franklin was a British scientist whose research was vital to understanding DNA.
e. This image later helped other researchers build their model of the DNA structure.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. B: Because I read about a young inventor and wanted to try my own experiment.
b. A: Excuse me, could you tell me about your science project?
c. A: That's inspiring. I'm sure you will get great results!
d. B: Sure. I'm studying how tiny plastic particles affect river water.
e. A: Why did you choose this topic?
qs.ex:
**Vì sao chọn C (b – d – e – a – c):**
Hội thoại bắt đầu bằng lời đề nghị lịch sự của A (b: "Could you tell me about your science project?"). B đáp lại ngay bằng "Sure" và giới thiệu đề tài (d). Tiếp theo, A hỏi lý do chọn đề tài (e: "Why...?"), B trả lời bằng "Because..." (a). Cuối cùng A nhận xét và chúc may mắn (c), đây là câu kết tự nhiên.

**Cần chú ý các đáp án còn lại:**
- A: "Because" (a) đứng trước câu hỏi "Why" (e), sai logic hỏi – đáp.
- B: mở đầu bằng d ("Sure...") khi chưa có câu hỏi nào, vô lý.
- D: e ("Why did you choose this topic?") xuất hiện trước khi B nêu đề tài, nên "this topic" chưa có nghĩa.

**Mẹo:** Tìm cặp hỏi – đáp, từ chỉ định (this, that) và các từ như "Sure", "Because" để xác định thứ tự.

Marie Curie is remembered as one of the greatest scientists in history, yet her path to fame was full of obstacles. Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, she grew up in a country where women were not allowed to study at university.

Determined to continue learning, Maria attended secret classes and worked as a **governess** to help pay for her sister's medical studies. In 1891, at the age of 24, she finally moved to Paris and enrolled at the Sorbonne. She was often hungry and cold, living in a tiny room, but she **persevered** and finished first in her physics exam.

In Paris, she married Pierre Curie, and together **they** worked in a poorly equipped laboratory, which was little more than an old shed. Nguyễn Minh Khang, a 17-year-old student from Cần Thơ, never imagined that a simple school visit to a science museum would change his life. There he read about Thomas Edison, who tested thousands of materials before inventing a practical light bulb. "If he could try again and again, so could I," Khang says.

The problem he wanted to solve was close to home. Every year, floods in the Mekong Delta damaged his neighbours' rice stores. Khang decided to build a low-cost moisture sensor that could warn farmers before the grain was **spoiled**. He set up a small laboratory in the corner of his garage, using old phone parts and a few cheap electronic components.

The early results were **disappointing**. His first twelve prototypes failed, and **one** even caught fire. However, Khang kept a notebook, recording every experiment and studying each mistake. After eight months and more than forty tests, his thirteenth model finally worked with 92% accuracy.

His innovative device won first prize at the provincial science contest in 2024, and a local cooperative now uses it in three villages. Khang's teachers praise his determination, but he insists that he is only following the example of the scientists he admires.

His next goal is to make the sensor solar-powered. "A breakthrough does not come in one day," he says. "You have to persevere, stay curious and never be afraid of failure."
qs.q: According to paragraph 1, what inspired Khang to start his project?
o: A documentary about floods in the Mekong Delta
A teacher's advice about a science contest
A competition held at his school
A story about Thomas Edison's repeated attempts that he read in a museum

(36) ______ When he was about five years old, his father showed him a small compass, and the boy was immediately fascinated. (37) ______ This experience, he later said, left a deep impression on him and made him believe that hidden forces lay behind everyday objects.

As he grew older, Einstein's curiosity turned toward mathematics. (38) ______ Consequently, he taught himself advanced problems long before his classmates had even heard of them. However, he disliked the strict, memory-based teaching at his school, so he often questioned his teachers instead of simply accepting their answers. (39) ______

In short, Einstein's childhood shows how powerful curiosity can be. (40) ______
qs.q: Chọn câu phù hợp nhất cho chỗ trống (40).
o: Because he never stopped asking "why", he eventually changed the way humans understand space, time and energy.
Because he accepted every answer, he never changed how people think about science.
Although he stopped asking "why", he eventually changed the way humans understand space, time and energy.
For example, his uncle changed the way humans understand space, time and energy.

When Linh Tran was eight years old, doctors told her family that she would lose her sight completely by the age of twelve. For many people, such news would end all hope for the future. For Linh, **it** was the beginning of a long **struggle** to prove that a disability does not decide who you are.

School was difficult at first. Her village had no books in Braille, and her classmates often did not know how to help her. Linh's mother read lessons aloud every evening, sometimes for three hours. Later, a local charity gave Linh a talking computer. With it, she could write essays, search for information and send emails on her own. Her grades rose quickly, and she finished high school as the top student in her district.

University brought new obstacles. Lecture slides were not **accessible**, and exams were not designed for students like her. After failing her first statistics test, Linh almost gave up. Instead, she asked her teachers for audio materials and formed a study group of five friends. Within a year, she was among the best students in her class. She graduated in 2012 with first-class honours in English literature.

Linh then won a scholarship to study abroad and earned a master's degree in education. Today, at thirty-two, she is a lecturer at a university in Hanoi, where she teaches about 120 students each semester. She also leads a project that has helped more than 300 visually impaired children get audio books.

"Every setback taught me something," Linh says. "I cannot see the faces of my students, but I can feel their curiosity." Her story inspires many young people to believe in themselves and never give up.
qs.q: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
o: The Best University Lecturers in Hanoi

At twenty-two, Maria Costa was one of the fastest swimmers in her country. She had won three national titles and dreamed of competing at the Olympic Games. Then, on a rainy night in 2016, a car accident changed everything.

Maria woke up in hospital with a badly injured spine and two broken legs. Doctors warned her that **she** might never walk normally again. The news was a heavy **blow**. For weeks she refused to speak to visitors, and she even asked her coach not to call her. "Water was my whole life," she remembers. "Without it, I felt lost."

The turning point came during rehabilitation. Every morning, a therapist helped her do simple exercises for six hours a day. At first, Maria could lift her leg only two centimetres. After four months, she could stand for one minute. Small victories like these gave her the courage to continue. President Ho Chi Minh is remembered as the father of modern Vietnam, but his story began with a young man who deeply loved his country.

Among the many heroes in Vietnamese history, the Trung sisters hold a special place. Trung Trac and Trung Nhi are remembered as the first women to lead a national uprising against foreign rule.

The sisters lived in the first century, when Vietnam was controlled by the Han Chinese. Heavy taxes and unfair laws made life very hard for local people. When Trung Trac's husband was killed by the rulers, her anger grew even stronger. In 40 AD, she and her sister called on the people to rise up.

The response was **remarkable**. Thousands of men and women joined the army, and many women became skilled commanders. Within a short time, the rebels took back around 65 citadels. The sisters were then crowned queens, and the country enjoyed a brief period of independence for about three years.

In 43 AD, the Han army returned with a much stronger force. According to legend, the sisters chose to end their lives in the Hat River rather than **surrender**. This sacrifice made **them** even more respected in the eyes of their people.

Today, the Trung sisters appear in many places in daily life. Streets in cities such as Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City carry their names, and temples in their honour stand in several provinces. Every year, people hold festivals to commemorate them with processions and traditional music. Their story shows young Vietnamese that courage has no gender, and that love for the homeland can inspire ordinary people to do heroic things.

o: The Trung Sisters: Heroines Remembered by the Nation

Many people believe that artists must begin training in childhood. The story of Maria Lenkova proves that this is not always true. She did not pick up a brush seriously until she was 58, yet today **her** paintings hang in galleries across Europe.

Maria was born in 1950 in a small farming village. Her family could not afford art lessons, so she spent her youth working in the fields and later as a **seamstress**. However, she always loved colour. She often drew flowers and neighbours on scraps of paper, simply for pleasure.

Her life changed when she retired in 2008. With more free time, she bought cheap paints and began to paint every morning. Because she had no teacher, she was completely **self-taught**. She learned by copying pictures in library books and by trying again whenever she made a mistake. Her inspiration came from the countryside of her childhood, with its golden wheat, old wooden houses and tired but smiling faces.

Recognition came slowly. In 2011, a visitor saw her work at a village fair and showed photographs to a gallery owner. A year later, Maria held her first exhibition with 25 paintings, and every one was sold. By 2020, her work had appeared in more than 30 exhibitions, and critics praised her honest, warm style.

Now in her seventies, Maria still paints daily. She says, "It is never too late to follow your talent. I only wish I had started sooner." Many admire her not only for her masterpieces but also for her courage to begin again.

In the mountain town of Valmora, old songs were once sung at every wedding and harvest festival. By the 1970s, however, most young people preferred pop music from the radio, and the traditional melodies were fading. One man refused to let them disappear. His name was Tomas Reyes.

Tomas was born in 1958 into a family of farmers. As a boy, he learned to play the wooden flute from his grandfather, who knew over 200 folk songs by heart. When his grandfather died in 1979, Tomas realised that this **treasure** of memory might die too. He decided to collect and record as **many** songs as he could.

For almost ten years, he travelled from village to village with a small tape recorder. He sat with elderly farmers, weavers and fishermen and listened patiently to their songs. In total, he gathered more than 350 melodies, many of which no one else remembered. He then wrote them down in notes and added short stories about their origins.

His own performances made the music popular again. At first, he played in small cafés, but audiences grew quickly. In 1994, his first album sold 40,000 copies, and he was invited to perform abroad. Critics praised the way he mixed traditional tunes with simple modern rhythms.

Today, Tomas teaches folk music to children in a free community school. Over 200 students have joined so far. "A song is a living memory," he often says. Thanks to his **dedication**, the voices of the past can still be heard by a new generation.

o: Why Farmers Make Better Musicians Than Singers
How Traditional Music Was Saved by One Dedicated Man
A Young Flute Player's Journey to Foreign Countries
The History of Pop Music in Mountain Towns

Tomas was born in 1958 into a family of farmers. As a boy, he learned to play the wooden flute from his grandfather, who knew over 200 folk songs by heart. When his grandfather died in 1979, Tomas realised that this **treasure** of memory might die too. He decided to collect and record as **many** songs as he could.

For almost ten years, he travelled from village to village with a small tape recorder. He sat with elderly farmers, weavers and fishermen and listened patiently to their songs. In total, he gathered more than 350 melodies, many of which no one else remembered. He then wrote them down in notes and added short stories about their origins.

His own performances made the music popular again. At first, he played in small cafés, but audiences grew quickly. In 1994, his first album sold 40,000 copies, and he was invited to perform abroad. Critics praised the way he mixed traditional tunes with simple modern rhythms.

Today, Tomas teaches folk music to children in a free community school. Over 200 students have joined so far. "A song is a living memory," he often says. Thanks to his **dedication**, the voices of the past can still be heard by a new generation.

o: He moved to the city to work as a singer.
He recorded his songs on a tape recorder.
He taught Tomas to play the wooden flute.
He died before Tomas was born.

Nguyen Minh Khoa, now one of Vietnam's most exciting strikers, did not begin his career in a famous academy. He started on a dusty street in a small town in Nghe An, kicking a plastic ball with his friends after school.
At the age of ten, Khoa joined a local youth team. His first coach quickly noticed his speed and his calm way of shooting. However, the family had little money, so Khoa often walked four kilometres to practise because he could not afford the bus. He later said that those long walks built the **endurance** he needed as a professional.
At sixteen, he entered a provincial club's youth academy. He trained six days a week, and he also spent extra hours on his weaker left foot. In his second season, he scored 18 goals in 22 matches, which helped his team win the regional tournament. **This achievement** attracted the attention of national selectors.
In 2021, Khoa received his first call-up to the national team. At first, he sat on the bench and rarely played. Instead of feeling **discouraged**, he studied the senior players and learned from every training session. His chance finally came in a qualifying match, when he scored the winning goal in the 89th minute.
Today, Khoa often visits his old street to meet children who play there. He tells them that talent is only the beginning. Teamwork, hard work and patience, he says, are what turn a dream into a career.
qs.q: What is the best title for the passage?
o: How to Choose a Good Football Academy
From a Dusty Street to the National Team: Khoa's Journey
The History of Football in Nghe An
Why Young Players Should Avoid Long Walks

When Tran Thu Ha lifted the gold medal at the Southeast Asian Games, millions of fans cheered. Few of them knew how many sacrifices stood behind that single moment.
Ha started playing badminton at the age of eight. By thirteen, **she** had moved to a sports training centre far from her family in Hai Phong. She saw her parents only during the Lunar New Year holiday. "I cried almost every night in the first year," she remembers.
Her daily routine was **demanding**. She woke up at 5 a.m. and ran five kilometres before breakfast. After that, she practised for four hours with her coach, repeating the same smash and footwork patterns hundreds of times. In the afternoon, she did strength exercises and watched videos of her opponents. She went to bed at 9 p.m. because rest was part of her training.
Discipline also meant giving up many things. Ha rarely ate sweets, spent little time on her phone and missed several friends' birthday parties. At eighteen, she even delayed university for two years so that she could compete in international events.
Her effort finally paid off. In 2022, she won three titles in one season and rose to 12th in the world rankings. She remains **modest** about her success. "I am not the most talented player," she says. "I am simply the most competitive person in the practice hall." Her story shows that a champion is built by daily choices, not only by victories.
qs.q: What is the best title for the passage?
o: How to Win Gold Medals at the Southeast Asian Games
Why Young Athletes Should Leave Their Families
The Hidden Sacrifices Behind a Badminton Champion
The History of Badminton in Vietnam

In the mountains of northern Vietnam, many villages lie far from the nearest school. Thirty years ago, a young teacher named Mr. Lam decided to change that.

After graduating from a teacher training college, Mr. Lam was offered a job in a town. Instead, he chose to work in a **remote** village called Pa Khoang. Every Monday morning, he left home at 4 a.m. and walked nearly twelve kilometres across hills, streams and muddy paths. The journey took almost four hours, and in the rainy season it was even longer.

When he arrived, he found only eleven children studying in a small bamboo hut. Many of their parents believed school was a waste of time because the children were needed in the fields. Mr. Lam visited each family, explained the value of education and promised to teach the children after their farm work. Slowly, parents began to trust **him**.

Over the next fifteen years, the number of students grew from eleven to over sixty. Mr. Lam taught reading, maths and basic science, and he also gave simple advice on health and hygiene. With help from villagers, he built a proper classroom with a tin roof.

Today, more than twenty of his former students have finished college. Some have become doctors, engineers and teachers. One of them, now a nurse, says, "He **devoted** his youth to us. We will never forget his dedication." Mr. Lam's story shows that one determined person can open the door to a better future for an entire community.

qs.p:
When Linh joined Grade 10, **she** rarely spoke in class. She sat in the back row, and her hands shook whenever a teacher called her name. She had good ideas, but fear kept them hidden.

Her literature teacher, Ms. Hanh, noticed this quickly. Instead of pushing Linh to speak in front of everyone, she offered quiet **guidance**. First, she asked Linh to share one opinion in a small group of three students. A week later, the group grew to six. Step by step, Linh's voice became stronger.

Ms. Hanh also encouraged Linh to join the school debate club. At first, Linh only took notes. After two months, she gave her first one-minute speech. It was not perfect, but Ms. Hanh praised her courage and gave useful feedback. "Every good speaker started with a **shaky** voice," she told her.

By Grade 11, Linh was speaking confidently in three debates each semester. Her team reached the city final, and she was chosen as the club's vice captain. She began helping new members who felt as nervous as she once had.

In Grade 12, Linh was elected president of the student council. At the opening ceremony, she spoke to more than 1,200 students without notes. Afterwards, she thanked Ms. Hanh with a handwritten card. "You believed in me before I believed in myself," she wrote.

Linh's story shows how a patient mentor can shape a young person's confidence and help hidden talents grow.

The Duties of a Student Council President
Why Literature Is the Most Important School Subject

Every morning at five o'clock, Nguyen Thi Hoa pushed a small cart onto a busy street in Da Nang. She was thirty-two, with two children and only 2 million dong in savings. Her cart sold just one thing: sticky rice with grilled pork, made from her grandmother's recipe.
At first, business was slow. Many days she earned less than 100,000 dong. However, Hoa listened carefully to her customers. **They** said the rice was **delicious** but the portions were too big for breakfast. She changed the size, lowered the price and added a small bag of homemade chili sauce. Within three months, she was selling over 150 portions a day.
In 2015, a customer filmed her cooking and shared the video online. It was watched more than two million times. Orders poured in from other cities, and Hoa faced a hard choice. She could keep her safe little cart, or she could take a risk and invest all her savings in a small kitchen. She chose the kitchen.
The **venture** grew steadily. By 2019, she had opened twelve shops and created a line of frozen meals sold in supermarkets nationwide. Her company now employs about 200 people, many of them single mothers like her.
Hoa says her success is not luck. 'I started with nothing, so I could only work harder and think smarter,' she explains. Today, she often visits schools to tell students that a big business can begin with one small cart and one honest idea.
qs.q: What is the best title for the passage?
o: From One Small Cart to a Successful Business
Why Single Mothers Should Avoid Risk
The Best Recipes in Da Nang
How Social Media Ruined Street Food

qs.p:
Minh Pham is now the founder of a successful software company, but his path was full of mistakes. At twenty-two, he left university to build a mobile game with two friends. They believed it would make them rich within a year.
The game was a disaster. Only 800 people downloaded it, and the team had spent nearly all of their 15,000 dollars of savings. Minh later admitted that **they** never asked players what they wanted. 'We built what we liked, not what people needed,' he says.
His second startup, a food delivery app, failed for a different reason. The idea was good, but the founders argued **constantly** and could not agree on money. After eighteen months, the company closed, and Minh owed his family 10,000 dollars. He remembers it as the lowest point of his life.
Instead of giving up, Minh wrote down every lesson he had learned. He promised to test ideas early, to choose partners carefully and to keep spending low. In 2018, he started a third company that helps small shops manage their stock. This time, he met fifty shop owners before writing a single line of code.
The results were very different. Within two years, the software had 5,000 users, and investors offered him 1 million dollars. Minh now tells young founders that failure is not the opposite of success. 'It is the price of learning,' he says, 'and you only pay it once if you pay attention.'
qs.q: What is the best title for the passage?
o: How to Make a Mobile Game
Learning from Failure on the Road to Success
The Best Food Delivery Apps in Vietnam

Dr Nguyen Thu Lan was born in a small town in the Red River Delta. As a child, she watched her grandmother suffer from a simple illness because the family could not afford a doctor. That memory stayed with her and shaped her future.
After graduating from medical university in 1995, Dr Lan had the chance to work in a big city hospital with a high salary. Instead, she chose to move to a **remote** mountain district near the northern border. At that time, the nearest clinic was a six-hour walk from many villages, and one doctor served about 8,000 people.
Dr Lan quickly realised that distance was only one problem. Many families had no clean water, and children often suffered from preventable diseases. She began to travel from village to village on a motorbike, carrying medicine in a small box. Over the years, she treated more than 30,000 patients, and most of **them** paid very little or nothing at all. She also trained 45 local women as health workers, so that people could get basic care even when she was away.
Her generosity **inspired** others. Medical students began to volunteer with her during their summer holidays, and a charity in Hanoi donated an ambulance and simple equipment. Thanks to these efforts, infant deaths in the district fell by almost half in fifteen years.
Now in her sixties, Dr Lan still works at the new health centre she helped to build. When people thank her, she smiles and says that she receives more than she gives. For her, true success is not money or fame, but seeing a healthy child run to school.

A woman who became famous for building the first health centre in Vietnam

qs.p:
When sixteen-year-old Tran Quang Minh visited his grandparents' village in Quang Binh last summer, he noticed something surprising. The small primary school there had only one shelf of old, torn books for more than 120 pupils. Minh felt sad, and he decided to act.
Back in the city, he started a book drive called Books for Little Hands. First, he asked his classmates to **donate** story books, dictionaries and picture books **they** no longer used. He also made posters and shared them on social media. Within two weeks, about forty students had joined him as volunteers, and the first boxes began to arrive.
The campaign grew quickly. Local bookshops gave discounts, and a printing company offered free labels for each book. By the end of October, the team had collected 2,600 books. They checked every one, repaired damaged pages and sorted them by age group. Then Minh and his friends delivered them to five rural schools, where they also built simple reading corners with wooden shelves.
The results were clear. Teachers reported that pupils borrowed books almost every day, and one school started a weekly reading club. A ten-year-old girl wrote Minh a letter saying that she had read her first whole book ever.
Minh says he is not a hero, just a student who wanted to help. His next goal is to collect 5,000 more books and create a small mobile library. His story shows that young people can make a difference when they combine kindness with careful planning.

Before 1939, Tomas Verne was a quiet young man who wrote gentle poems about rivers and gardens. Few people read them. His first collection, **published** when he was twenty-two, sold only 150 copies, and one newspaper called his style "pleasant but forgettable."
Everything changed when war reached his country. Verne was sent to a medical unit near the front line, where he spent four years caring for wounded soldiers. At night, by candlelight, he began to write short poems on scraps of paper, old envelopes and even the backs of medical forms. These poems were no longer about gardens. They described fear, hunger, friendship and the small hopes that kept people alive.
His **literary** style also changed. Instead of long, decorated sentences, he chose simple words and short lines. A single poem might have only twenty words, yet readers felt its emotional power at once. Critics later said that the war had taught him to remove everything **unnecessary** from his writing.
Soldiers began to copy his poems by hand and pass them around. By 1943, at least six camps had their own handwritten collections. When the war ended, a publisher gathered about 90 of **these** poems into one book. It sold more than 200,000 copies in its first year and was translated into twelve languages.
In his memoir, Verne explained that he had not looked for a new voice. "It found me," he wrote, "when I stopped trying to sound like a poet and started listening to people." Today, his work is taught in schools as an example of how suffering can turn into art.

o: Why Poetry Is Less Popular Than Novels
A Guide to Writing Poems About Nature
How War Transformed a Poet's Writing and Brought Him Success
The Best Medical Care During Wartime

qs.p:
At nineteen, Mai Anh Tran became one of the youngest novelists in her country. Her first book, "The Rice Field Letters," is based on the life of her grandmother, Bà Hạnh, and it has already become a bestseller with more than 80,000 copies sold.
The idea began during a summer holiday in the countryside. Mai Anh found a box of old letters under her grandmother's bed. Curious, she asked about **them**, and Bà Hạnh spent the next three weeks telling stories about her childhood, the years of **hardship** after the war and the long journey she made to the city at the age of sixteen. Mai Anh filled two notebooks with her notes.
Turning these memories into a novel was not easy. The facts alone were not enough, so she used her imagination to build scenes, conversations and characters. She chose a narrative told in the first person, as if her grandmother were speaking directly to the reader. "I wanted people to hear her voice," Mai Anh explained.
Writing took fourteen months. She worked every evening after school and rewrote the first chapter eleven times. Her grandmother read each draft and sometimes laughed, sometimes cried, and often corrected small details about food, clothes and songs from that time.
Since its publication, the book has received many messages from readers. Many of them say it encouraged them to interview their own grandparents. Mai Anh is now planning a second novel, but she says her first book taught her the most important lesson: "Every family holds a story that deserves to be told."

In 1975, a small Japanese woman named Junko Tabei did something that many people believed was impossible. On 16 May, she became the first woman to reach the summit of Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world at 8,849 metres.

Tabei was born in 1939 in a small town in Japan. She climbed her first mountain at the age of ten and never lost her love for the outdoors. Later, she founded a women's climbing club because many men's clubs at that time did not welcome female members. Some people even said that women should stay at home instead of risking their lives on mountains.

The Everest expedition was full of danger. Twelve days before the summit attempt, an avalanche suddenly hit the camp at about 6,300 metres while the climbers were sleeping. Tabei was buried in the snow and lost consciousness. Fortunately, her Sherpa guide dug her out, and only a few days later she continued the climb. Her body was in pain, but her **determination** was stronger.

Near the top, the team had to cross a narrow icy ridge with deep drops on both sides. The air was so **thin** that every step felt like a great effort. Despite **these difficulties**, Tabei and her guide reached the summit in the afternoon.

Tabei's success did not end there. She later became the first woman to climb the highest peak on every continent, completing the challenge in 1992. She also worked to protect mountain environments from rubbish left by climbers. Her story shows that bravery, patience and a strong will can break even the hardest boundaries.

Mae Jemison grew up in Chicago, but many astronauts come from much smaller places. Take the example of an imaginary student, Daniel, from a quiet farming town of only 3,000 people. His path shows how a distant dream can become reality.

As a boy, Daniel spent his evenings looking at the night sky from the roof of his family's barn. The town had no science museum, so **he** borrowed library books about planets and rockets. At the age of twelve, he built a simple telescope from a cardboard tube and two cheap lenses. That small project **convinced** him that he wanted to explore space.

Daniel worked very hard at school, especially in mathematics and physics. He won a scholarship to study engineering at university, where he also learned to fly small planes. After graduating, he joined a research team and spent six years designing equipment for satellites. During this time, he applied to become an astronaut three times and was rejected twice. Each failure taught him something new about patience and preparation.

Finally, among more than 12,000 applicants, he was one of only twelve people selected. Training lasted two years. He practised underwater to imitate weightlessness, studied foreign languages and learned how to repair machines in emergencies.

Today, Daniel has completed two missions and spent over 200 days orbiting the Earth. He often returns to his hometown to talk to students. His message is simple: where you start does not decide where you can go. With curiosity, effort and courage, even a child from a small town can reach the stars.

o: How to Build a Telescope at Home
Why Farming Towns Need Science Museums
The History of Space Travel in the World
From a Small Town to Space: A Dream Made Real

After graduating, he joined a research team and spent six years designing equipment for satellites. During this time, he applied to become an astronaut three times and was rejected twice. qs.p:
For young people who grow up in a multicultural city, diversity is not a topic studied in textbooks but an everyday reality. On the bus to school, they hear several languages being spoken; in the canteen, they see classmates eating foods that their grandparents might never have tried. Because this **exposure** begins early, it tends to feel natural rather than strange, and it quietly shapes how these teenagers understand the world around them.
One of the most noticeable effects is a greater willingness to question assumptions. When a teenager befriends someone whose family follows a different religion or celebrates different festivals, general statements about "those people" quickly lose their power. Researchers who study adolescent attitudes have observed that personal friendships across cultural lines are often more effective at reducing prejudice than any lecture, since **they** replace **abstract** ideas with real individuals. Such young people also tend to develop stronger empathy, as they have repeatedly had to imagine situations from another person's point of view.
However, living among many cultures is not automatically beneficial, and it can sometimes bring tension. Misunderstandings may arise when customs about politeness, humour or family responsibilities differ, and young people who feel pressure to choose between their heritage and the majority culture may struggle with their identity. What makes the difference is often the support they receive, which includes teachers who encourage open discussion and families who value both the old and the new. Those who receive such support usually learn to move comfortably between cultures, drawing strength from each of them.
It follows that schools and communities should do more than simply place students from different backgrounds in the same room. They could organise joint projects, invite young people to share their family traditions, and train teachers to handle sensitive topics with confidence. If such efforts are made consistently, multicultural cities will produce not only tolerant citizens but also flexible thinkers who are ready to cooperate with people anywhere in the world.

Festivals have always been more than days off work or school; they are occasions when people gather to share what matters to them. In many countries, a single festival can attract thousands of visitors, **who** might otherwise never speak to one another. This makes festivals a powerful way of connecting people from different parts of society.
One reason for this is that festivals give everyone something to do together. Whether people are cooking traditional dishes, decorating streets or watching a parade, they work side by side towards a **common** goal. These shared activities often lead to conversations, and conversations in turn create friendships that last long after the celebration has ended.
Festivals also help communities understand cultures other than their own. In large cities, for instance, residents often join the New Year celebrations of neighbouring groups, where they try **unfamiliar** foods, listen to new kinds of music and learn the stories behind each custom. <u>Because they are invited as guests rather than as outsiders, they usually feel welcome and curious instead of nervous.</u>
Finally, festivals remind people that they belong to something larger than their own families. Organisers who invite several communities to take part together often find that old misunderstandings disappear quickly. In this way, a few days of music, colour and laughter can strengthen a community for the whole year.

qs.p:
The Lunar New Year, which is celebrated in China, Vietnam, Korea and many other countries, began as an ancient farming festival that marked the end of winter and the hope for a fruitful spring. According to one popular legend, villagers used red decorations and loud noises to frighten away a monster, and **this** explains why red envelopes and firecrackers are still associated with good fortune today.
Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is one of the most important events in India and among Hindu communities worldwide. It **commemorates** the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and it is often linked with the return of Prince Rama to his kingdom after years of exile. <u>During the festival, families light small oil lamps, decorate their doorways with colourful patterns and exchange sweets with neighbours, which strengthens the bonds between them.</u>
Eid al-Fitr, on the other hand, is observed by Muslims in countries such as Indonesia, Egypt and Turkey to mark the end of Ramadan, a month of fasting and reflection. People gather for special prayers in the morning, wear their best clothes and visit relatives, while many also give money or food to those in need, as **generosity** is a central value of the occasion.
Although these festivals differ in origin and ritual, they share some striking similarities. Each one encourages people to reunite with their loved ones, to express gratitude and to look forward to the future with hope, which shows that very different cultures can value the same human feelings.

the ancient farming tradition in many countries
the fact that villagers used red decorations and loud noises to frighten away a monster

qs.p:
Every February, the Rio Carnival transforms Brazil's second-largest city into a stage on which millions of people dance, sing and celebrate for several days. Although the event grew out of local street parties that were influenced by European, African and Indigenous traditions, it has become a global phenomenon that attracts more than a million international visitors each year. The most famous attraction is the parade in the Sambadrome, where samba schools compete with elaborate floats, dazzling costumes and music that can be heard across the neighbourhood.
The economic impact of this spectacular occasion is **considerable**. Hotels, restaurants and airlines report their busiest weeks of the year, while street vendors, taxi drivers and craftspeople earn a substantial share of their annual income during the festivities. According to city authorities, the carnival generates billions of reais and creates tens of thousands of temporary jobs, **many of which** are filled by residents from lower-income communities.
Nevertheless, the benefits are not shared equally, and the event also presents serious challenges. Prices for accommodation rise **sharply**, public services come under pressure, and large crowds produce enormous amounts of waste that the city must clear within days. Furthermore, some critics argue that the commercial side of the festival, including expensive tickets and sponsorship deals, risks pushing ordinary Brazilians away from a tradition that originally belonged to them.
In conclusion, the Rio Carnival demonstrates how a cultural event can support a local economy while strengthening national pride. To make its success more sustainable, however, organisers should invest in environmental protection, offer affordable tickets for residents and ensure that small businesses receive a fair portion of the profits. If these measures are adopted, the carnival can continue to delight visitors while remaining a genuine expression of the community that created it.

Every February, the Rio Carnival transforms Brazil's second-largest city into a stage on which millions of people dance, sing and celebrate for several days. Although the event grew out of local street parties that were influenced by European, African and Indigenous traditions, it has become a global phenomenon that attracts more than a million international visitors each year. The most famous attraction is the parade in the Sambadrome, where samba schools compete with elaborate floats, dazzling costumes and music that can be heard across the neighbourhood.
The economic impact of this spectacular occasion is **considerable**. Hotels, restaurants and airlines report their busiest weeks of the year, while street vendors, taxi drivers and craftspeople earn a substantial share of their annual income during the festivities. According to city authorities, the carnival generates billions of reais and creates tens of thousands of temporary jobs, **many of which** are filled by residents from lower-income communities.
Nevertheless, the benefits are not shared equally, and the event also presents serious challenges. Prices for accommodation rise **sharply**, public services come under pressure, and large crowds produce enormous amounts of waste that the city must clear within days. Furthermore, some critics argue that the commercial side of the festival, including expensive tickets and sponsorship deals, risks pushing ordinary Brazilians away from a tradition that originally belonged to them.
In conclusion, the Rio Carnival demonstrates how a cultural event can support a local economy while strengthening national pride. To make its success more sustainable, however, organisers should invest in environmental protection, offer affordable tickets for residents and ensure that small businesses receive a fair portion of the profits. If these measures are adopted, the carnival can continue to delight visitors while remaining a genuine expression of the community that created it.

qs.p:
Few forces have shaped what we eat as profoundly as migration. When people leave their homeland, they cannot pack their villages, their markets or their grandmothers' kitchens, but they can carry the memory of flavours, and that memory often proves remarkably **durable**. Wherever migrants settle, they tend to recreate the dishes of home, which gradually become part of the new country's culinary landscape.
Pizza is a classic example. It began as an **inexpensive** staple food for working families in Naples, and it travelled across the Atlantic with millions of Italians who left poverty behind in the late nineteenth century. In American cities, bakers adapted it to local taste by adding thicker crusts and generous toppings, so that the dish eventually returned to Italy in a form its inventors would scarcely have recognised. Sushi followed a similar path after Japanese communities settled in places such as California and Brazil, where the scarcity of traditional ingredients inspired inventions like the avocado-filled roll.
Pho tells a slightly different story, since its global journey was driven largely by upheaval rather than by economic opportunity. After 1975, many Vietnamese families resettled in France, the United States and Australia, and **those** who opened small restaurants introduced customers to a fragrant noodle soup that required hours of patient cooking. Initially, diners regarded it as exotic, but its comforting simplicity won them over, and it is now served in cities where few people could once have pronounced its name.
These examples suggest that food is never fixed; it evolves each time it crosses a border. Instead of worrying about whether a dish is entirely authentic, we might ask who created it, what hardships shaped it and what it reveals about the people who carried it. Restaurants, schools and food writers could help by telling these stories alongside the menu, so that every meal becomes not only a pleasure but also a lesson in shared human history.

Every family has a dish that appears on special occasions and brings everyone to the table. In many cultures, such a dish is much more than a meal, because **it** carries the memory of ancestors who first prepared it and the values they hoped to pass on. When a grandmother teaches her grandchild how to make it, she is also handing down a piece of the family's history.
Family recipes are rarely written down in exact detail. Instead, they are usually learned by watching, tasting and helping in the kitchen, and this is why the instructions often include phrases such as "a handful of herbs" or "cook until it smells right". <u>Such unclear measurements may frustrate beginners, but they encourage close contact between generations, which is precisely what keeps the tradition alive.</u>
For people who live far from their homeland, these recipes have an even deeper meaning. Cooking a familiar dish in a foreign kitchen can reduce **homesickness** and remind them who they are, especially when the right ingredients are difficult to find. Many migrants say that the smell of a childhood meal makes them feel connected to a place they cannot visit.
Because modern life is busy, however, some of these recipes are at risk of disappearing. Young people often rely on fast food or ready-made meals, and fewer of them learn the skills their parents once took for granted. To **prevent** this loss, families can record their recipes in notebooks or videos and cook together regularly, so that their cultural identity continues to be tasted for generations.

Many migrants say that the smell of a childhood meal makes them feel connected to a place they cannot visit.
Because modern life is busy, however, some of these recipes are at risk of disappearing. Young people often rely on fast food or ready-made meals, and fewer of them learn the skills their parents once took for granted. To **prevent** this loss, families can record their recipes in notebooks or videos and cook together regularly, so that their cultural identity continues to be tasted for generations.

qs.p:
Learning a second language is often seen as a school requirement, but it is much more than that. When students begin to understand another language, they gain access to a whole new way of thinking, which allows them to see the world from a different point of view. For example, a learner of Spanish may discover that certain feelings are described in ways that English simply cannot express.
In addition, a language is closely connected to the history and values of the people who speak **it**. <u>Reading a novel, watching a film or listening to a song in its original language lets learners experience a culture directly instead of through a translation, which may lose some of the meaning.</u> Because of this, many students who study a language become curious about the traditions, humour and daily habits of its speakers.
Language skills also make it easier to form real friendships. Travellers who can speak even a little of the local language usually receive a warmer welcome, as people **appreciate** the effort that has been made to communicate with them. Likewise, those who become bilingual often find it easier to adapt to **unfamiliar** situations, which helps them study or work abroad with greater confidence.
Of course, reaching a high level takes time, and learners will inevitably make mistakes along the way. However, each mistake is a step forward, and every new word opens another door. Ultimately, the person who learns a second language does not simply gain a skill but also gains a wider, more generous understanding of humanity.

Although spoken languages are studied carefully, body language is often taken for granted, even though it can convey attitudes and emotions more powerfully than words. Consequently, a harmless movement made in one country may be interpreted quite differently elsewhere.
Consider the familiar "thumbs up", which signals approval in many Western countries but is considered rude in parts of the Middle East. Similarly, nodding usually means "yes", whereas in Bulgaria and some neighbouring regions it can mean the opposite, a fact that has left many visitors thoroughly confused. Even the amount of eye contact varies **considerably**: while it demonstrates honesty and confidence in many societies, it may be regarded as disrespectful when directed at elders or superiors in others.
Such differences can have serious consequences in business, education and diplomacy. A manager who misreads a colleague's silence or a lack of eye contact may wrongly conclude **that** the person is uninterested, whereas the colleague may in fact be showing respect. Likewise, students on exchange programmes sometimes feel hurt by gestures that their hosts never intended as insulting. These incidents, which seem trivial at first, can gradually damage trust if nobody takes the trouble to clarify them.
It is therefore essential that people prepare themselves before dealing with unfamiliar cultures. Schools and employers should include practical training on non-verbal communication, and travellers ought to research local customs in advance. Above all, when confusion arises, we should respond with curiosity rather than judgement, asking politely what was meant. By doing so, we can turn potential conflict into an opportunity for mutual understanding.

qs.q:
Dear Mrs Lan,
a. You had spent a year in Australia as an exchange student, so I hope you can give me some tips on dealing with culture shock.
b. Last month I was awarded a scholarship to study there for a year, although I had never lived overseas before.
c. Could we meet next week so that I can ask you a few more questions?
d. I am writing to ask for your advice about the exchange programme I will join in Canada next September.
e. Since then, I have often wished I knew more about how to adjust to life with a host family.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Mai: Why don't you ask your host family for a quieter room?
b. Mai: Hi Tom, you look tired. Did something happen last night?
c. Tom: Yes, I couldn't sleep. I wish my homestay were less noisy.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. Indeed, some of them had never been away from their families before, so they feel homesick during the first weeks.
b. Studying abroad gives students valuable chances to broaden their horizons.
c. In conclusion, despite these difficulties, the experience helps young people become more independent and open-minded.
d. First, they live in a new environment in order to learn a foreign language more quickly.
e. However, adapting to a different culture is not always easy, and many students experience culture shock when they arrive.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Jack: That's impressive. Do you feel nervous about living overseas?
b. Linh: Jack, I've just heard that I got a scholarship to study in Japan!
c. Linh: A little. I wish I could take my whole family with me, but I'll video call them every day.
d. Linh: I had spent months practising Japanese before I took the interview.
e. Jack: Congratulations! What did you do to win it?

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. In addition, they learn local customs, such as table manners, that textbooks rarely explain.
b. For this reason, students should keep an open mind and talk honestly with their hosts in order to adjust quickly.
c. A homestay is one of the best ways for exchange students to experience a new culture.
d. Nevertheless, some students had expected a perfect stay, so they feel disappointed when problems appear.
e. By living with a host family, students can practise the local language every day.

qs.p:
Studying overseas is an exciting opportunity, but it is rarely as simple as packing a suitcase and boarding a plane. Many exchange students arrive full of enthusiasm, only to discover that everyday habits, such as how people greet each other, how they queue, or how directly they express disagreement, (12) ______. This unexpected difference often leads to culture shock, a feeling of confusion and anxiety that can affect even the most confident learners.
Fortunately, culture shock is usually temporary, and there are several ways to reduce its effects. First of all, students who keep an open mind and treat every misunderstanding as a chance to learn tend to adapt more quickly than (13) ______. In addition, living with a host family allows them to observe local customs closely and to ask questions in a natural setting, (14) ______. Joining clubs or volunteering also helps, because shared activities build friendships faster than classroom conversation alone.
Of course, feeling homesick from time to time is perfectly normal. (15) ______ Therefore, the best approach is to balance old connections with new ones. Over time, students who follow this advice usually find that the experience not only improves their language skills but also (16) ______.

o: are differing greatly from those at home
differ greatly from those at home
is greatly different from those at home
greatly differ with those at home
