qs.p:
When I landed in Toronto last September as a seventeen-year-old exchange student, I believed that my years of studying English had prepared me for anything. Within a week, however, I realised that **fluency** in grammar is very different from fluency in daily life. Classmates spoke quickly, used slang that I had never met in textbooks, and laughed at jokes that I could not understand, which made me feel strangely invisible.
The real culture shock, nevertheless, came from small, unspoken rules rather than from language. In Vietnam, I had been taught to listen quietly and avoid challenging teachers, whereas my Canadian teachers expected students to interrupt politely, question ideas and share personal opinions. At first I interpreted this openness as disrespect, and my silence in class was mistaken for a lack of interest. Meanwhile, my host family's habit of eating dinner at five-thirty and discussing problems directly at the table seemed almost shocking compared with the **indirect** communication I was used to.
The turning point arrived in November, when I was struggling with homesickness and nearly decided to book an early flight home. My host mother, who had noticed my mood, did not offer advice; instead, she invited me to bake with her and asked me to teach her a Vietnamese recipe. Cooking spring rolls together gave me a sense of pride, and **it** reminded me that I had something valuable to contribute rather than merely adjust to. From then on, I began to speak up in class, join the debate club and accept that mistakes were a natural part of learning.
Looking back, I believe that culture shock should be seen as a stage of growth rather than a failure. Schools that organise exchange programmes could prepare students better by offering workshops on cultural differences and by connecting newcomers with former exchange students. Likewise, future travellers should arrive with curiosity instead of fixed expectations, because the willingness to adapt is ultimately what transforms an unfamiliar country into a second home.

o: smoothness and ease in using a language

Homestay programmes, in which teenagers live with a local family in another country, have become increasingly popular among secondary school students. Unlike a hotel or a dormitory, a host family offers a real home where visitors share meals, chores and conversations. This close contact gives young people an **authentic** view of daily life that no textbook can provide.
One of the greatest benefits of a homestay is that it encourages independence. Away from their parents for the first time, students have to manage their own time, keep their rooms tidy and solve small problems without immediate help. <u>For example, a student who misses a bus must learn to ask for directions and find another route, and this kind of experience builds confidence far more effectively than advice from adults.</u>
Homestays also make teenagers more open-minded. Because **they** live with people whose habits, beliefs and traditions are different from their own, they are often forced to question assumptions that they have never examined before. Many students report that, after sharing a family's festival or trying unfamiliar food, they feel more curious about other cultures and less likely to judge them quickly.
Of course, the experience is not always easy, and some students feel homesick or uncomfortable during the first few weeks. Nevertheless, most of them say that these difficulties were worth the effort, since they returned home more mature, more **tolerant** and better prepared for life in a multicultural world.

Homestay programmes, in which teenagers live with a local family in another country, have become increasingly popular among secondary school students. Unlike a hotel or a dormitory, a host family offers a real home where visitors share meals, chores and conversations. This close contact gives young people an **authentic** view of daily life that no textbook can provide.
One of the greatest benefits of a homestay is that it encourages independence. Away from their parents for the first time, students have to manage their own time, keep their rooms tidy and solve small problems without immediate help. <u>For example, a student who misses a bus must learn to ask for directions and find another route, and this kind of experience builds confidence far more effectively than advice from adults.</u>
Homestays also make teenagers more open-minded. Because **they** live with people whose habits, beliefs and traditions are different from their own, they are often forced to question assumptions that they have never examined before. Many students report that, after sharing a family's festival or trying unfamiliar food, they feel more curious about other cultures and less likely to judge them quickly.
Of course, the experience is not always easy, and some students feel homesick or uncomfortable during the first few weeks. Nevertheless, most of them say that these difficulties were worth the effort, since they returned home more mature, more **tolerant** and better prepared for life in a multicultural world.

Homestays are mainly designed to improve students' cooking skills.
All students feel comfortable from the first day of a homestay.

qs.p:
National costumes are much more than beautiful clothes, because each of them reflects the history, values and way of life of the people who created **it**. <u>The Vietnamese ao dai, for example, developed over several centuries from earlier long tunics, and it took its modern, fitted shape in the twentieth century when designers began to make it follow the lines of the body more closely.</u>
The Japanese kimono has an even longer history, which can be **traced** back more than a thousand years. Its straight lines and wide sleeves were originally designed for comfort and movement, but over time the garment became a symbol of social status and good taste. The colours, seasonal designs and the way the belt is tied can tell an observer about the wearer's age, the occasion and even the time of year.
In Korea, the hanbok is admired for its graceful curves and bright colours, which were once used to show a person's rank and marital status. Although the style has changed **gradually**, many of its traditional features have survived because Koreans regard them as an important part of their heritage.
Today, these three outfits are worn mainly on festive days, yet they continue to remind people where they come from. By choosing to wear them, younger generations show that they value the skills of the craftspeople who made them and that they are proud of the cultures that these garments symbolise.

National costumes are much more than beautiful clothes, because each of them reflects the history, values and way of life of the people who created **it**. <u>The Vietnamese ao dai, for example, developed over several centuries from earlier long tunics, and it took its modern, fitted shape in the twentieth century when designers began to make it follow the lines of the body more closely.</u>
The Japanese kimono has an even longer history, which can be **traced** back more than a thousand years. Its straight lines and wide sleeves were originally designed for comfort and movement, but over time the garment became a symbol of social status and good taste. The colours, seasonal designs and the way the belt is tied can tell an observer about the wearer's age, the occasion and even the time of year.
In Korea, the hanbok is admired for its graceful curves and bright colours, which were once used to show a person's rank and marital status. Although the style has changed **gradually**, many of its traditional features have survived because Koreans regard them as an important part of their heritage.
Today, these three outfits are worn mainly on festive days, yet they continue to remind people where they come from. By choosing to wear them, younger generations show that they value the skills of the craftspeople who made them and that they are proud of the cultures that these garments symbolise.

qs.q:
Dear Ms Linh,
a. a. I am writing to ask whether our class could visit the folk music exhibition at your cultural centre next month.
b. b. It is the traditional instruments that interest us most, especially those made in villages where craftsmanship has been passed down for generations.
c. c. We would also be grateful if a performer could play a few folk songs live for us during the visit.
d. d. Could you please let me know which days are available for a group of thirty students?
e. e. Thank you very much for considering our request.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Tom: It is the stage design that impressed me most, not the singers.
b. b. Mai: Did you enjoy the concert of folk songs last night?
c. c. Tom: Yes, I did, and I'd love to go to another one.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Intangible heritage, such as folk songs and traditional performances, is a living part of a community's identity.
b. b. However, it is often at risk because young people are drawn to modern entertainment.
c. c. Indeed, many folk songs are said to have been forgotten in villages where they were once sung daily.
d. d. This is why schools and museums are encouraged to organise activities that inspire young learners.
e. e. In conclusion, protecting intangible heritage requires effort from both communities and institutions.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Linh: Have you seen the new art exhibition downtown?
b. b. Nam: Not yet. Is it the one whose paintings were made by young local artists?
c. c. Linh: Yes, it is. It is believed to be the biggest youth exhibition in the city.
d. d. Nam: That sounds great. Shall we go this weekend, when the gallery opens late?
e. e. Linh: Perfect. I'll book the tickets online tonight.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. The masterpiece is thought to have been painted in the late nineteenth century by a self-taught artist.
b. b. It shows a village market where people from different cultures trade goods and share stories.
c. c. Many critics believe that it is the artist's use of colour that makes the scene so lively.
d. d. As a result, the painting, which now hangs in a national museum, attracts thousands of visitors every year.
e. e. In short, its artistic value lies in how it celebrates cultural diversity.

qs.p:
Throughout history, art has never stayed inside the borders of a single country. When traders, travellers and migrants moved from one region to another, they carried not only goods but also songs, patterns and stories, (12) ______. For example, the pottery of the ancient Silk Road combined Chinese, Persian and Central Asian designs, which is why many pieces from that period look so unusual and so beautiful at the same time.

In modern times, this exchange has become faster and more visible, mainly because of the internet. A young musician in Hanoi can listen to a folk song from Mexico in the morning and, by the evening, (13) ______. Likewise, painters in Europe have long been inspired by Japanese prints, and (14) ______. Some people worry that such borrowing may weaken local traditions; however, it often does the opposite, because (15) ______.

In conclusion, art grows richer when cultures meet, listen and respect one another. (16) ______.

Street art, especially large murals, has become one of the most powerful ways for communities to express who **they** are. Unlike paintings in a gallery, which people must travel to see, murals appear on ordinary walls, so everyone who walks past can enjoy them for free. This openness is a major reason why they feel so close to local residents.
Many murals are created with the help of the people who live nearby. <u>In some neighbourhoods, artists begin by interviewing older residents about local history, and then they turn those memories into colourful images of old markets, rivers or traditional costumes.</u> As a result, the finished work is not just decoration but a shared story that everybody **recognises** as their own. Children who grow up in front of such a wall often feel proud of their neighbourhood, because it reminds them where their families come from.
Street art can also bring communities together in difficult times. After a natural disaster or a long period of conflict, a painted wall may carry messages of hope and **unity**, which encourages people to rebuild their lives. In addition, the creation process itself gives young volunteers a chance to cooperate, learn new skills and take responsibility for their surroundings.
Of course, not everyone agrees that every wall painting is welcome, and artists must respect the owners of buildings as well as the feelings of local people. When they listen carefully and work with the community, however, murals can turn grey, empty spaces into meaningful places that people love and protect.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Linh: Yes, he asked me whether I was from China, and I told him I was Vietnamese.
b. Linh: Actually, I felt a bit upset because he assumed things about me too quickly.
c. Mark: Did anything unpleasant happen at the international club yesterday?

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Nam: I see. If he had known you better, he wouldn't have judged you so quickly.
b. Hoa: He told me that girls were not good enough at science to join the robotics team.
c. Nam: That is such a harmful stereotype! What did you say to him?
d. Nam: You look worried, Hoa. What did your classmate say to you this morning?
e. Hoa: I asked him why he believed that, and he couldn't give me any reason.

Dear Mr Tran,
a. I am writing to suggest a short workshop on prejudice and respect for our Grade 12 students.
b. Last month, a new student told me that some classmates had asked her whether she could speak proper Vietnamese because of her accent.
c. She was so hurt that she hardly spoke in class for a week.
d. If the school had organised such an activity earlier, she might not have felt so isolated.
e. Could you please ask the students to prepare short role-plays about equality and open-minded behaviour for the event?
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. A stereotype is a fixed and oversimplified idea about a group of people, and it often leads to serious misunderstanding.
b. However, many people accept such ideas without checking whether they are true.
c. This habit can develop into bias, which makes them treat others unfairly.
d. Indeed, discrimination at school or work often begins with a small misconception that nobody challenges.
e. In conclusion, being open-minded and inclusive is the first step towards building a society based on equality.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. Many teenagers think they are too young to fight prejudice, but this belief is wrong.
b. In fact, students are old enough to challenge unfair jokes and to show respect for classmates from different backgrounds.
c. For example, a teacher once told her class not to laugh at anyone's accent, and the classroom became much friendlier.
d. This shows that small actions can have such a strong effect that the whole atmosphere changes.
e. Therefore, if every student had the courage to speak up, our schools would be more inclusive places.

qs.p:
Most of us have heard **sweeping** statements about other nationalities, such as "Germans are always strict" or "Brazilians are born to play football." Although such comments may seem harmless, even humorous, they are **misleading** because they reduce millions of individuals to a single, simplified image. No country is home to people who all think, behave or dress in the same way.
Stereotypes usually develop from limited experience, which is then repeated by films, advertisements and social media. When a person sees only one version of a culture, **they** may believe it represents the whole truth. <u>Over time, this belief can turn into prejudice, and prejudice can lead to discrimination in schools, workplaces and public life, which damages both the people targeted and society as a whole.</u>
So how can we challenge these misconceptions? First, we should ask ourselves where our opinions come from and whether we have any real evidence for them. Second, getting to know people personally, either through travel, online exchanges or friendships at school, shows us how varied any group really is, and it often surprises us.
Finally, we can speak up politely when someone makes an unfair generalisation. This does not require us to argue; it can be as simple as saying, "That hasn't been my experience." By choosing curiosity over assumption, we help build a world in which people are judged by their actions rather than by their passports.
qs.q: The word "**sweeping**" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ____.

qs.p:

Although such comments may seem harmless, even humorous, they are **misleading** because they reduce millions of individuals to a single, simplified image. No country is home to people who all think, behave or dress in the same way.
Stereotypes usually develop from limited experience, which is then repeated by films, advertisements and social media. When a person sees only one version of a culture, **they** may believe it represents the whole truth. <u>Over time, this belief can turn into prejudice, and prejudice can lead to discrimination in schools, workplaces and public life, which damages both the people targeted and society as a whole.</u>
So how can we challenge these misconceptions? First, we should ask ourselves where our opinions come from and whether we have any real evidence for them. Second, getting to know people personally, either through travel, online exchanges or friendships at school, shows us how varied any group really is, and it often surprises us.
Finally, we can speak up politely when someone makes an unfair generalisation. This does not require us to argue; it can be as simple as saying, "That hasn't been my experience." By choosing curiosity over assumption, we help build a world in which people are judged by their actions rather than by their passports.

qs.p:
Today's classrooms are more diverse than ever, bringing together students whose languages, beliefs, family structures and economic circumstances differ widely. While this diversity is a valuable resource, it can also become a source of tension if schools fail to address the bias that sometimes lies beneath everyday interactions. Creating an inclusive environment, therefore, is not an optional extra but a basic responsibility of every educational institution.
One of the most effective starting points is the curriculum itself. When textbooks and lessons present only a **narrow** range of perspectives, students from minority backgrounds may feel invisible, whereas their peers may unconsciously absorb the idea that some cultures matter more than others. By including diverse authors, historical viewpoints and examples, teachers can help all learners recognise that knowledge is shaped by many communities, which strengthens mutual respect.
Equally important is the way adults respond to discrimination. Clear anti-bullying policies, accessible reporting systems and consistent consequences send a strong message that unfair treatment will not be tolerated. Teachers also need regular training so that they can identify **subtle** forms of prejudice, such as low expectations for certain groups, **which** are often unintentional but nonetheless harmful.
Finally, students themselves should be given a genuine voice. Peer-led clubs, mentoring schemes and cultural showcases allow young people to learn from one another and to challenge misconceptions in a natural, friendly way. In conclusion, schools that combine inclusive teaching, firm policies and active student participation can ensure that every learner feels safe, valued and capable of success. Governments and communities should support this work with adequate funding, because the benefits of equality in education extend far beyond the school gates.

Dear Ms Hoa,
a. a. During the visit, we would like to see the Imperial City and a few other tourist attractions in the area.
b. b. I would be grateful if you could send me the price and the tour schedule by the end of this week.
c. c. I am writing to ask for your help with a sightseeing tour that my class is going to take in Hue next month.
d. d. Could you recommend a local guide who will explain the history of these places in simple English?
e. e. We are arriving at the airport on the morning of 12 May, and we are staying in a small hotel near the Perfume River.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Lan: Yes, go straight along this street, then turn left at the traffic lights.
b. b. Mark: Thanks a lot! I'm going to meet a local guide in front of the gate at ten.
c. c. Mark: Excuse me, is this the right way to the Temple of Literature?

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. For this reason, many governments are going to introduce limits on the number of visitors to the most popular sites.
b. b. The tourism industry plays an important role in the economy of many countries, but it also affects local culture.
c. c. In conclusion, tourism will help preserve cultural heritage only when it is managed carefully.
d. d. However, too many tourists can damage a famous tourist attraction if nobody controls the crowds.
e. e. On the one hand, visitors bring money to a destination, and this creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Nam: A small souvenir from your country would be perfect, and they will welcome you warmly.
b. b. Emma: Nam, I'm visiting a village in Hoi An tomorrow. Is there any etiquette I should know?
c. c. Emma: Great, I'm going to take some postcards of London, then.
d. d. Nam: Yes, you should take off your shoes before you enter a local home.
e. e. Emma: Good to know. And should I bring a gift for the family?

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. First of all, guides know the history behind each monument, so they can tell stories that books rarely mention.
b. b. Thanks to this knowledge, travellers walk through the streets with more confidence and respect.
c. c. In short, hospitality and understanding from local people make a destination memorable.
d. d. A good local guide can turn an ordinary sightseeing trip into an unforgettable experience.
e. e. Moreover, they introduce the customs of the community, which helps visitors behave politely in unfamiliar places.

qs.p:
Mass tourism has transformed many small communities around the world, and its impact on local culture is both encouraging and troubling. On the positive side, the arrival of large numbers of visitors creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport, (12) ______. qs.p:
For decades, the global tourism industry measured its success by the number of arrivals, yet many communities that welcomed those crowds gained little beyond crowded streets and rising prices. Responsible tourism challenges this model by asking a different question: who actually benefits from a journey? Its supporters argue that travel should leave a place at least as healthy, culturally and economically, as it was before visitors arrived, and they **encourage** travellers to choose businesses that are owned and run by local people.
One practical way to achieve this is to employ residents as local guides, who can explain the history of a tourist attraction in a way that no brochure can match. Because guides are members of the community, the money they earn stays in the neighbourhood, and **their** knowledge is valued rather than ignored. In several mountain regions, for example, elderly craftspeople now teach weaving or woodcarving in small workshops, which has persuaded younger relatives to learn skills that were once expected to vanish. Visitors who buy a handmade souvenir directly from its maker, rather than a factory-produced copy, support this process in a very direct manner.
Responsible tourism also protects traditions by setting boundaries that respect the wishes of residents. Some villages, for instance, ask visitors not to enter during private ceremonies, while others limit the daily number of people allowed into a **fragile** heritage site. Although such rules may seem inconvenient, they help preserve the atmosphere and the authenticity that attracted travellers in the first place. In return, communities are generally more willing to share their hospitality, which makes the experience richer for everyone.
Ultimately, responsible tourism is not a special type of holiday reserved for a few idealistic travellers; it is a habit that anyone can adopt. Before booking a trip, visitors should research the customs of their destination, choose locally owned accommodation and spend their money where it will do the most good. If governments, businesses and travellers all share this responsibility, tourism can become a powerful partner in protecting cultural heritage rather than a threat to it.

Travelling to a new country is exciting, but behaviour that seems perfectly polite at home may cause confusion or even **offence** elsewhere. Learning the basics of local etiquette before you go shows respect for your hosts, and it often leads to warmer and more helpful encounters. Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Mark: Yes, I'd like to visit a craft village and interview the artisans about keeping their traditions alive.
b. b. Lan: Great idea! Even though many young people are leaving, some villages still preserve their crafts very well.
c. c. Lan: Have you decided what to do for our project on globalisation and cultural identity?

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Linh: Hardly had we opened this morning when a group ordered twenty bowls, so it will take about a week.
b. b. Tom: Hello, I'd like to have a small bowl made at your workshop as a souvenir.
c. c. Tom: That's fine. Not only will I come back to pick it up, but I'll also bring my friends to learn pottery.
d. d. Linh: Of course. Would you like to have your name painted on it as well?
e. e. Tom: Yes, please. How long will it take to get it done?

Dear Mr Tran,
a. a. We would like to visit on a Saturday morning and have your artisans show us the weaving process.
b. b. I am writing to ask for your help with our school project on globalisation and cultural identity.
c. c. Could you please let me know whether 15 November is convenient for you?
d. d. In particular, not only is your village famous for its silk, but it also has young artisans who keep the craft alive.
e. e. Our class is studying how craft villages preserve their traditions in spite of the influence of mass-produced goods.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. As a result, some minority languages and rituals have become endangered.
b. b. In conclusion, integration into the world need not mean losing what makes a nation unique.
c. c. Globalisation has connected countries more closely than ever before, but it also puts many local cultures under pressure.
d. d. However, even though globalisation is powerful, communities can preserve their identity by teaching traditions at school and supporting craft villages.
e. e. Indeed, young people who watch foreign films and use global apps may gradually assimilate into one global lifestyle.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Some villages, however, have had their products promoted online, which helps them reach customers worldwide.
b. b. Hardly had tourists begun to visit these villages when cheap factory copies appeared in many shops.
c. c. Thanks to this, the villages keep their traditions alive while earning a stable income.
d. d. Many craft villages in Viet Nam are facing a difficult choice between tradition and modern markets.
e. e. This made it hard for artisans to sell their handmade products at fair prices.

qs.p:
In an age when goods, ideas and people move across borders faster than ever before, every nation faces a difficult question: how can it take part in the global community without losing what makes it unique? Integration brings clear benefits, including new technology, wider job opportunities and (18) ______. However, it also exposes countries to strong outside influences, and these may slowly change the way people dress, speak and celebrate.
This risk is greatest for small communities, (19) ______. When young people choose foreign music, fast food and fashion simply because they seem modern, local customs can be forgotten within a single generation. Some minority groups have already been pressured to assimilate into the dominant culture, and in the process they have (20) ______.
Nevertheless, integration and cultural identity are not opposites. (21) ______ Schools can teach national history and folk arts, governments can support festivals and craft villages, and families can pass on stories at home. In this way, a nation does not build a wall around itself; instead, it enters the world (22) ______, which is the strongest foundation for lasting cooperation.
qs.q: Chọn câu phù hợp nhất cho chỗ trống (18).
o: a better understanding of other cultures
a better understood of other cultures

Thanks to cheap flights, international trade and the internet, products, ideas and lifestyles that were once limited to a single region can now reach millions of people within hours. A teenager in Hue, for example, can listen to Korean pop music in the morning and cook an Italian recipe in the evening.
Social media has **accelerated** this process dramatically. Platforms such as TikTok and YouTube allow ordinary users to share their customs with a worldwide audience, which has helped some traditions gain unexpected popularity. A folk song performed by a village girl may go viral overnight, and craftspeople who once sold only in their local market can now find customers abroad.
At the same time, the same tools can weaken the very cultures **they** promote. <u>Because global trends are so visible, young people may feel that their own traditions are old-fashioned and therefore not worth learning.</u> Languages spoken by small groups are particularly at risk, since children often prefer the **dominant** languages they see online, and festivals may be shortened or changed to suit the tastes of tourists.
This does not mean that we should reject modern technology. Instead, communities can use it wisely by recording elders' stories, teaching traditional skills through online videos and encouraging young people to be proud of their roots. If we do so, globalisation can become a partner in protecting diversity rather than a threat to it.

qs.p:
Across the world, thousands of languages and traditional crafts are disappearing at an **alarming** rate. Linguists estimate that a language falls silent roughly every few weeks, and with it goes a unique way of understanding nature, history and human relationships. Craft traditions face a similar fate, since many of them rely on techniques that were never written down and are known only to a handful of ageing masters.
It would be easy to blame young people for this **decline**, as they are often seen as being more attracted to global trends than to local heritage. Yet recent projects suggest that the younger generation may in fact be the most powerful force for revival. Many young people are bilingual or even multilingual, they are skilled at using digital tools, and they have the energy to experiment. In several regions, teenagers have created mobile apps to teach minority languages, while **others** have filmed elderly artisans at work and published the footage online, thereby preserving skills that might otherwise have vanished.
Moreover, young people can give old traditions a contemporary appeal that makes them relevant to their peers. A designer who adds traditional embroidery patterns to modern jackets, or a musician who combines ethnic instruments with electronic beats, shows that heritage need not be locked in a museum. Such creativity attracts new audiences, and it can also provide a sustainable income, which is essential if craft villages are to retain their young members rather than lose them to the cities.
To build on this potential, schools, governments and communities should offer genuine support. Minority languages could be taught as optional subjects, funding could be provided for apprenticeships with master artisans, and online platforms could be encouraged to give visibility to local content. Above all, adults should listen to young people instead of simply instructing them. If the guardians of tomorrow are given both respect and resources, endangered languages and crafts have a real chance not merely to survive, but to flourish.

qs.p:
When the Nguyen family in Da Nang looked inside their kitchen bin one evening in January, they were shocked to find that nearly everything in it was plastic. Mrs Lan, a primary school teacher, had read that Vietnam produces millions of tonnes of plastic waste each year, much of which ends up in rivers and, eventually, in the sea. She decided that her household, which includes two teenagers and a grandmother, should try to reduce its **contribution** as far as possible within twelve months.
The first change was surprisingly simple. The family replaced plastic carrier bags with cloth ones, bought rice and spices in their own jars from a local market, and stopped using bottled water after installing a filter at home. Although these steps seemed **minor**, they cut the amount of waste by almost half within three months, **which** encouraged everyone to go further.
The harder challenge came later, because many products in supermarkets are wrapped in layers of packaging that cannot be avoided easily. Mr Nguyen therefore began to buy fresh vegetables directly from farmers, while the children made shampoo bars and cleaning liquids from natural ingredients. Peels and leftovers were turned into compost for the balcony garden, so very little organic waste reached the landfill. By December, the family filled only one small bag of rubbish every month.
Their experience suggests that dramatic results do not require expensive equipment or special knowledge, but rather patience and teamwork. Local authorities could support similar efforts by encouraging shops to sell goods without unnecessary packaging and by organising workshops on waste sorting. If more households followed this example, the pressure on our overflowing landfills would fall noticeably, and our rivers would be cleaner for the next generation.
qs.q: The word "**contribution**" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ____.

Single-use plastic bags first became popular in the 1970s, when supermarkets began to offer them as a cheap and **convenient** alternative to paper. They were light, waterproof and strong, so customers quickly accepted them, and within a few decades billions were being produced every year. Few people imagined at that time that such a useful invention would become a global environmental problem.
The main difficulty is that plastic bags are not biodegradable. Instead of disappearing, **they** break into tiny pieces called microplastics, which can remain in the ocean for hundreds of years. <u>Because the wind carries lightweight bags from streets and landfills into rivers, a large number eventually reach the sea.</u>
Marine animals suffer greatly as a result. Sea turtles, for example, often mistake floating bags for jellyfish, which are part of their natural diet, and the plastic blocks their stomachs. Birds and fish can also become trapped in bags, while microplastics enter the food chain and may even return to humans through seafood.
In response, many countries have introduced taxes or complete bans on single-use bags, and the results have been **encouraging**. In some places, bag use has fallen by more than 80 percent. Individuals can help too by carrying reusable shopping bags and by choosing eco-friendly products, which shows that every person has a part to play in protecting the oceans.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Linh: Sure. If we switch off the lights and fans when we leave, we will cut our electricity bill a lot.
b. Nam: Our class electricity bill was higher than usual last month. Do you have any idea how to reduce it?
c. Linh: Great idea! Let's make a poster to remind everyone about it.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. Mai: Not really. I usually leave my laptop in standby mode overnight. Is that a problem?
b. Tom: Yes, it is. Devices in standby mode still use power, so turning them off completely is better.
c. Mai: I see. If I unplugged everything before going to bed, would it make a real difference?
d. Tom: Have you checked how much power your appliances use at home, Mai?
e. Tom: It would. Over a year, you could save quite a lot of money and reduce your carbon footprint, too.

Dear Mr Tran,
a. I would be grateful if you could install energy-efficient LED bulbs in all classrooms, because they are cheaper to run than the old ones.
b. I am writing on behalf of the Green Club to suggest some ways of saving energy at our school.
c. If the school agrees, we will help to check the rooms and remind students to switch off equipment after lessons.
d. First, we noticed that many lights and projectors stay on even when classrooms are empty.
e. In addition, we think installing solar panels on the roof would be the best long-term solution to reduce our electricity bill.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. Indeed, a household that relies only on old appliances may pay far more than one using energy-efficient models.
b. Saving energy at home is one of the simplest ways to protect the environment and our wallets.
c. However, buying new devices is not the only solution, because small habits also matter.
d. For example, switching off lights and avoiding standby mode can reduce power consumption noticeably.
e. In conclusion, we can lower both our bills and our carbon footprint by choosing wisely and using electricity carefully.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. Good insulation is therefore one of the most effective ways of improving energy efficiency in a house.
b. Many homes lose a large amount of heat through walls, windows and roofs.
c. This means families have to use heaters or air conditioners more often, which raises their electricity bills.
d. If owners installed better insulation, their homes would stay warmer in winter and cooler in summer.
e. As a result, they would depend less on fossil fuels and produce a smaller carbon footprint.

qs.p:
Living in a school dormitory means sharing rooms, sockets and bills with many other students, so even tiny wasteful habits can add up quickly. Fortunately, most of them are easy to change, and the first step is simply to notice how much electricity we use every day. Leaving lights on in an empty room, for example, may seem harmless, but (18) ______, the power consumption of the whole building rises sharply.
One of the most effective habits is to switch off lights, fans and air conditioners (19) ______. Likewise, chargers, laptops and kettles should be unplugged after use, because many appliances keep drawing power in standby mode even when they appear to be off. (20) ______, which makes it much easier to cut the supply at bedtime.
In addition to these daily routines, small improvements to the room itself help too. Opening curtains during the day provides natural light, while closing them in the afternoon keeps the heat out, (21) ______. Finally, if every floor chooses a monitor (22) ______, students will see the results of their efforts and feel motivated to continue. In this way, a few simple habits can protect both the school budget and the environment.

qs.p:
For many families, the electricity bill is one of the largest monthly expenses, and **it** tends to rise every year as people buy more devices. Smart home technology offers a practical solution because it allows households to monitor and control their energy use instead of guessing where it goes. A smart meter, for instance, shows exactly how much power each appliance consumes, which helps owners identify the habits that cost them the most.
Another useful feature is automation. Smart thermostats learn when family members are at home and adjust the temperature **accordingly**, so air conditioners do not run all day in empty rooms. Similarly, smart plugs can switch off televisions and game consoles that would otherwise stay in standby mode, a small change that quietly saves a surprising amount of electricity over a year.
Lighting is also easier to manage with this technology. Sensors turn lights on only when someone enters a room, and energy-efficient LED bulbs can be dimmed from a phone, which reduces both **waste** and cost. <u>Some families even connect their systems to solar panels, allowing them to use the electricity they generate during the day before taking any from the grid.</u>
Of course, smart devices are not free, and some people worry that the initial cost is too high. However, experts point out that the savings usually repay the investment within a few years, and the technology also lowers a household's carbon footprint. For this reason, more and more families regard smart homes not as a luxury but as a sensible long-term choice.

qs.p:
Although Vietnam has made remarkable progress in extending electricity to almost every household, many **remote** villages in mountainous and island areas still suffer from unstable supply. Connecting these communities to the national grid is often extremely expensive, since power lines must cross rugged terrain and serve only a small number of people. As a result, solar energy, which is **abundant** across much of the country, has become an increasingly attractive alternative.
For rural families, the benefits of solar panels are both practical and immediate. A modest system can power lights, a fan and a phone charger, which allows children to study safely after dark and gives parents more time for work. Farmers have also started to use solar-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, a change that reduces fuel costs and makes their income more reliable. Moreover, because sunlight is a renewable resource, **these** installations produce electricity without the pollution caused by diesel generators.
Nevertheless, several obstacles remain. The initial cost of equipment is still high for low-income households, and batteries need regular maintenance that few villagers have been trained to carry out. Without proper support, systems that break down may be abandoned, which wastes both money and public trust. Some projects have addressed this problem by offering small loans and by teaching local technicians how to repair the equipment, and their experience suggests that community involvement is essential.
In conclusion, solar power has the potential to transform rural life, but its success depends on more than technology alone. Authorities should expand financial support, provide long-term training and encourage cooperation between villages, businesses and schools. If these measures are adopted together, rural communities will not only gain reliable electricity but also contribute to Vietnam's wider goal of reducing its carbon footprint.

Dear Mr Tran,
a. a. I am writing to ask whether our school could set up a carpool scheme for students who live in the same area.
b. b. Many of my classmates, who commute by motorbike, arrive late because the traffic congestion near the school gate is so heavy.
c. c. If the scheme works, it will reduce exhaust fumes, which are a serious cause of air pollution in our neighbourhood.
d. d. I would therefore be grateful if you could let us use the school noticeboard to organise the groups.
e. e. I am the monitor of Class 12A, and I have been looking for ways to make our daily trip to school greener.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Lan: He said that the bus was too crowded, so he decided to cycle instead.
b. b. Lan: Why did Nam arrive at school so early today?
c. c. Minh: He told me yesterday that he would pedal to school every morning from now on.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Indeed, cities that have reliable buses and metro lines often see far fewer private cars on their streets.
b. b. However, public transport will only attract passengers if it is clean, safe and frequent enough.
c. c. Public transport is one of the most effective ways of reducing emissions in large cities.
d. d. In conclusion, investing in good public transport benefits both the environment and people's daily lives.
e. e. This is because a single bus can carry as many people as dozens of cars, which means less fuel is burnt.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Tom: That is true, but my cousin, who lives in Hue, said that her fuel-efficient car costs very little to run.
b. b. Anna: Because it is such a long way that I cannot walk, and the bus does not stop near my house.
c. c. Tom: Why do you drive to work every day when petrol is so expensive?
d. d. Anna: I see. Maybe I should buy a fuel-efficient car, or join a carpool with my neighbours.
e. e. Anna: Then you should think about it, because pedestrians and cyclists will also enjoy cleaner air.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Walking and cycling are the greenest ways to travel, especially for short journeys in towns and cities.
b. b. Moreover, regular exercise helps people stay healthy, which is a benefit that cars can never offer.
c. c. Unfortunately, many cities are not safe enough for pedestrians, so people prefer to drive.
d. d. Therefore, governments should build wider pavements and cycle lanes that protect people from heavy traffic.
e. e. These activities produce no exhaust fumes, so they do not add to air pollution.

qs.p:
For almost two years, I rode my motorbike to school every morning because I believed it was the fastest way to get there. However, after a heavy rainstorm left me stuck in traffic for nearly an hour, I began to wonder whether there was a better option. My cousin, (12) ______, suggested that I try it for a month, and I reluctantly agreed.
The first week was not easy, since I had to get up earlier and learn the bus timetable. Nevertheless, I soon noticed several advantages. (13) ______, I could review my vocabulary or listen to music during the journey. Moreover, I no longer breathed in so many exhaust fumes at crowded junctions, (14) ______.
The change has also affected my wallet and my attitude towards the environment. I spend much less on fuel and parking, and I have realised that one full bus can replace dozens of private vehicles, (15) ______. Of course, public transport is not perfect, because buses are sometimes late and crowded at rush hour. (16) ______, and I would encourage other teenagers to give it a try.

qs.p:
In recent years, electric buses have started to appear on the streets of Bangkok, Jakarta, Manila and Hanoi, and their popularity is growing faster than many experts predicted. This trend is largely driven by the **severe** air pollution that affects densely populated cities in the region. Because traditional diesel buses release large amounts of exhaust fumes and carbon dioxide, local governments have come under increasing pressure to find cleaner alternatives.
Apart from reducing emissions, electric buses offer economic advantages that are difficult to ignore. Although they cost **considerably** more to purchase than conventional vehicles, they require less maintenance and use electricity, which is usually cheaper than diesel over time. In addition, they run almost silently, which makes crowded neighbourhoods more pleasant for residents, who have long complained about the constant roar of engines.
Nevertheless, the transition is far from straightforward. Many cities still lack enough charging stations, and the electricity that powers the buses is sometimes generated by burning coal, **which** partly cancels out the environmental benefit. Furthermore, the high initial investment can be a serious obstacle for municipalities with limited budgets, so they often depend on foreign loans or private partnerships.
To make the most of this technology, authorities should combine the purchase of electric buses with investment in renewable energy and reliable charging networks. They should also improve routes and ticketing systems so that more commuters are persuaded to leave their private vehicles at home. If these measures are carried out together, electric buses could become the backbone of a cleaner and less congested urban future.

Cycling to school is becoming a popular choice among students in large cities, and it is easy to understand why. A bicycle allows teenagers to avoid long queues of vehicles, so they often arrive faster than classmates who travel by car. It also provides daily exercise, which helps students stay **fit** and concentrate better during lessons.
Besides personal benefits, cycling is good for the community. Every student who pedals instead of being driven reduces traffic congestion near school gates, **where** parents' cars often block the road at busy times. In addition, bicycles produce no emissions, so a large group of cyclists can make a real contribution to cleaner air in the neighbourhood.
However, riding a bike in crowded urban areas also involves serious challenges. <u>Narrow streets, fast motorbikes and careless drivers can put cyclists at risk, especially when there are no separate bike lanes.</u> Bad weather and the lack of safe parking can also **discourage** students, who worry that their bicycles might be stolen.
Fortunately, these problems can be solved if schools and local authorities work together. They could build protected bike lanes, provide secure parking areas and organise safety classes for new riders. Once students feel confident and protected, more of them will probably choose to cycle, and the whole city will benefit.

Living in an apartment does not mean giving up the pleasure of growing your own food. In fact, a balcony of only two or three square metres can become a productive mini garden, (18) ______.
The first step is to observe how much sunlight your balcony receives during the day. Herbs such as mint, basil and coriander grow well with four to six hours of light, whereas tomatoes and chillies need more. Once you know this, you can select containers, (19) ______. Old plastic bottles, buckets and wooden boxes work perfectly, and reusing them also reduces waste. Vertical shelves are another smart solution because (20) ______.
Growing your own vegetables brings several benefits. First, you decide what goes into the soil, so you can avoid chemical pesticide and enjoy truly organic produce. Second, your food travels only a few steps from the pot to the kitchen, which means zero food miles. Finally, tending plants is a relaxing hobby that teaches patience, especially for busy students (21) ______. (22) ______, and the pride of eating something you have grown yourself is hard to beat.

In recent years, an increasing number of teenagers around the world have chosen to reduce the amount of meat in their meals, and some have given it up completely. Although vegetarian eating has existed for centuries, it is young people who are now **driving** its popularity, largely because they have grown up with constant news about climate change and environmental damage.
One major reason for this trend is that raising animals for food requires huge amounts of land, water and energy. Many students have learned that a plant-based meal usually produces far fewer greenhouse gases than a meat-based one, so **they** see their daily lunch as a simple way to make a difference. <u>Social media has also played an important role, since it allows them to share colourful recipes and inspire friends who might otherwise never have tried tofu or lentils.</u>
However, switching to a sustainable diet is not as easy as it sounds. Teenagers are still growing, which means that they need enough protein, iron and vitamins to stay healthy. Nutrition experts therefore advise them to eat a wide variety of beans, nuts, seeds and green vegetables, and to check with a doctor if they are **worried** about missing nutrients.
Fortunately, schools and families can help. Canteens that offer tasty vegetarian options make it easier for students to change their habits, while parents who cook together with their children often discover that healthy meals can be both cheap and delicious. In this way, a personal choice can gradually grow into a shared lifestyle.

qs.p:
Restaurants are often admired for their creativity, yet behind the kitchen door many of them throw away a surprising amount of perfectly edible food. Studies suggest that a typical restaurant **discards** several tonnes of food each year, which not only wastes money but also contributes to greenhouse gas emissions when the waste rots in landfills. Since the problem begins long before a dish reaches the table, solutions must start with careful planning.
One of the most effective strategies is accurate forecasting. By recording how many customers visit on different days and which dishes they order, managers can predict demand and buy only what is needed. Some restaurants now use simple software that analyses these records, and owners who have adopted **it** report that their ingredient costs have fallen noticeably. Likewise, designing menus around seasonal and locally grown produce reduces spoilage, because such ingredients are **fresher** on arrival and usually require less storage and transport.
Portion size and kitchen practice matter as well. Customers frequently leave large amounts of leftovers on their plates, so offering smaller portions or allowing diners to choose half servings can prevent unnecessary waste. Meanwhile, chefs can make creative use of items that would normally be discarded, such as turning vegetable peels into stock or using stale bread in puddings. Staff training is crucial here, since even the best system fails if employees are unaware of why it matters.
In conclusion, reducing food waste in restaurants requires cooperation between owners, chefs and customers, but it is neither expensive nor complicated. Businesses should begin by measuring how much food they throw away, set realistic targets and review their progress regularly. Governments could encourage this by rewarding restaurants that donate surplus food or publish their waste figures. If these steps become common practice, the food industry could move significantly closer to a truly sustainable diet for everyone.

qs.p:
Every year, millions of plastic bottles are **discarded** after a single use, and many of them end up in landfills or in the ocean, where they may remain for hundreds of years. Linh Tran, a twenty-six-year-old designer from Da Nang, decided that she could no longer ignore this problem. Having worked in a fashion studio for three years, she realised that her skills could be used to give such waste a purpose, so she began experimenting with bottles collected from her neighbourhood.
Her method is surprisingly simple but requires great care. First, the bottles are cleaned and cut into thin strips, which are then softened with heat and woven into a strong, **flexible** fabric. Linh sews this material into handbags and backpacks, adding lining made from second-hand cloth that she buys at local markets. Because the finished bags are lightweight, waterproof and extremely durable, customers often say **they** are more practical than those made from leather or cotton.
What makes her work remarkable is not only the product itself but also the message behind it. Linh works with a small team of local women, many of whom had difficulty finding stable jobs before, and she organises weekend workshops in which teenagers learn how to transform rubbish into fashion. In her view, creativity is a renewable resource that costs nothing, whereas raw materials such as oil, which is needed to produce new plastic, are limited.
Linh's story suggests that sustainable fashion does not have to be expensive or complicated. Schools could invite young designers to run similar workshops, and city councils could place collection points in busy areas so that more bottles are saved from the bin. If consumers also choose upcycled products instead of cheap, disposable ones, the demand for new raw materials would fall, and projects like hers could grow far beyond a single small studio.

Every year, millions of plastic bottles are **discarded** after a single use, and many of them end up in landfills or in the ocean, where they may remain for hundreds of years. Linh Tran, a twenty-six-year-old designer from Da Nang, decided that she could no longer ignore this problem. Having worked in a fashion studio for three years, she realised that her skills could be used to give such waste a purpose, so she began experimenting with bottles collected from her neighbourhood.
Her method is surprisingly simple but requires great care. First, the bottles are cleaned and cut into thin strips, which are then softened with heat and woven into a strong, **flexible** fabric. Linh sews this material into handbags and backpacks, adding lining made from second-hand cloth that she buys at local markets. Because the finished bags are lightweight, waterproof and extremely durable, customers often say **they** are more practical than those made from leather or cotton.
What makes her work remarkable is not only the product itself but also the message behind it. Linh works with a small team of local women, many of whom had difficulty finding stable jobs before, and she organises weekend workshops in which teenagers learn how to transform rubbish into fashion. In her view, creativity is a renewable resource that costs nothing, whereas raw materials such as oil, which is needed to produce new plastic, are limited.
Linh's story suggests that sustainable fashion does not have to be expensive or complicated. Schools could invite young designers to run similar workshops, and city councils could place collection points in busy areas so that more bottles are saved from the bin. If consumers also choose upcycled products instead of cheap, disposable ones, the demand for new raw materials would fall, and projects like hers could grow far beyond a single small studio.

o: How to Start a Fashion Studio in Da Nang
From Waste to Wardrobe: A Young Designer's Upcycling Journey
Why Leather and Cotton Bags Are Disappearing
The Dangers of Plastic Pollution in the Ocean

When we put used glass, paper and metal into a recycling bin, most of us do not think about what happens next. In fact, the journey is long and carefully **organised**. Trucks take the materials from collection points to sorting centres, where workers and machines separate them by type and remove anything that cannot be recycled.
Glass is crushed into small pieces called cullet, which is then melted at a high temperature. Because cullet melts more easily than raw materials such as sand, factories use less energy when they include **it**. The melted glass is shaped into new bottles and jars, and this process can be repeated many times without losing quality.
Paper follows a different path. It is mixed with water to make a soft pulp, and then the ink and dirt are removed. After that, the pulp is pressed and dried into new sheets, which may become newspapers, boxes or notebooks. <u>However, paper fibres become shorter each time they are recycled, so the same paper can only be reused a limited number of times.</u>
Metal, especially aluminium and steel, is sorted with powerful magnets or electric machines before being melted down. Recycling aluminium needs far less energy than producing it from raw ore, which makes it one of the most **efficient** forms of recycling. Understanding this process can encourage people to sort their rubbish properly, since clean and well-separated materials are much easier to transform into new products.

For most visitors, a national park is a place to relax, but for a forest ranger it is a workplace that never closes. Minh, (18) ______, usually begins his day before sunrise, when he checks the equipment and plans the route with his team. They then walk for several hours, carefully looking for signs of illegal activity such as snares, fresh stumps or unfamiliar footprints.
Although patrolling is the most visible part of the job, it is far from the only one. Rangers also record the animals they meet, and (19) ______ whether a population of endangered species is growing or shrinking. Tropical forests cover only a small part of the Earth's surface, yet **they** are home to more than half of all known land species. This **extraordinary** biodiversity exists because the warm, wet climate allows countless plants, insects and animals to live closely together. Each of them plays a role, so the whole ecosystem depends on a **delicate** balance.
Unfortunately, this balance is being destroyed by deforestation. Large areas are cleared every year for farms, roads and timber, and when trees disappear, the animals that depend on them lose their habitat as well. <u>Some species, such as orangutans, need huge areas of continuous forest, so even a small road can separate families and make it difficult for them to find food or mates.</u>
The damage does not stop there. Trees hold water in the soil and absorb carbon dioxide, which means that their loss can lead to erosion, floods and a warmer climate. Moreover, once a species has reached extinction, it can never be brought back, and the medicines or foods it might have offered to humans are lost forever.
Fortunately, solutions exist. Governments can create protected reserves and punish illegal logging, while companies can use certified timber. Ordinary consumers can help too by choosing products that do not harm forests, which encourages businesses to change their practices.

qs.p:
Two decades ago, the future of the langurs living in a limestone forest in northern Vietnam looked **bleak**. Hunting for traditional medicine and the clearing of land for farming had reduced their numbers to fewer than one hundred individuals, and many experts feared that they would soon vanish. Today, however, the population has more than doubled, and the project responsible is often cited as a model for the whole region.
The turning point came when conservationists decided that protecting animals was impossible without the support of local people. Instead of simply banning activities, they hired former hunters as forest guards, giving them a stable income and a new sense of pride. At the same time, the project built small schools and funded scholarships, which persuaded many families that the survival of the primates would bring **tangible** benefits to their own children.
Science played an equally important role. Researchers used camera traps and regular surveys to monitor the groups, and **their** data showed which cliffs and trees were most vital for feeding and sleeping. As a result, rangers were able to concentrate patrols on these areas, and degraded land nearby was restored through reforestation with native species, which gradually reconnected isolated groups and strengthened their genetic diversity.
The lesson from this success is clear: lasting conservation requires cooperation among communities, scientists and authorities. Other countries facing similar threats should therefore invest in education and fair livelihoods as much as in law enforcement. Moreover, young people can contribute by spreading awareness and refusing to buy products made from endangered wildlife. If such efforts continue, these remarkable animals may one day be removed from the list of critically endangered species.

Science played an equally important role. Researchers used camera traps and regular surveys to monitor the groups, and **their** data showed which cliffs and trees were most vital for feeding and sleeping. As a result, rangers were able to concentrate patrols on these areas, and degraded land nearby was restored through reforestation with native species, which gradually reconnected isolated groups and strengthened their genetic diversity.
The lesson from this success is clear: lasting conservation requires cooperation among communities, scientists and authorities. Other countries facing similar threats should therefore invest in education and fair livelihoods as much as in law enforcement. Moreover, young people can contribute by spreading awareness and refusing to buy products made from endangered wildlife. If such efforts continue, these remarkable animals may one day be removed from the list of critically endangered species.

Camera Traps: The Newest Tool for Hunters
The Decline of Traditional Medicine in Vietnam
Cooperation and Science: How a Vietnamese Project Brought Langurs Back from the Brink

Dear Mr Tran,
a. a. I am writing to ask whether our class could organise a water-saving campaign at school next month.
b. b. If the school had repaired the leak near the canteen last year, we would not have wasted so much freshwater.
c. c. We would also like to install a rainwater tank, and we could use it for irrigation in the school garden, couldn't we?
d. d. Could you please give us permission and let us know a convenient time to discuss the plan with you?
e. e. Last week we noticed that a tap in the girls' toilet is almost always dripping, which is quite a serious problem.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Lan: Yes, I should have. If I had known about the shortage, I would have turned it off earlier.
b. b. Minh: You left the tap running while brushing your teeth again, didn't you?
c. c. Minh: Don't worry, just remember to turn it off from now on.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Water scarcity is becoming one of the most serious environmental problems in many parts of the world.
b. b. Indeed, long droughts have dried up rivers and lakes, so farmers often cannot find enough water for irrigation.
c. c. However, only a small part of the planet's water is freshwater that people can actually use.
d. d. This is why governments encourage households to adopt water-saving habits and to purify wastewater for reuse.
e. e. In conclusion, if we had protected our water sources earlier, we would not be facing such a crisis today.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Hoa: Yes, but it hardly ever rains here in summer, so we rely on it quite a lot, don't we?
b. b. Nam: Our water bill is much higher this month. Do you know why?
c. c. Hoa: Maybe there is a leak somewhere. If we had checked the pipes last month, we would have noticed it.
d. d. Nam: You're right. Why don't we collect rainwater for the garden instead of using tap water?
e. e. Nam: Good point. Then let's call a plumber first and buy a rainwater tank later.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Many cities now face water shortages because their populations are growing rapidly.
b. b. As a result, some of them have built plants that purify wastewater so that it can be used again.
c. c. For example, treated water is often used to clean streets and to supply irrigation systems in parks.
d. d. Although this technology is fairly expensive, it is extremely useful in dry regions.
e. e. Therefore, if more cities had invested in it earlier, they would be much less dependent on rainfall today.

qs.p:
The Mekong Delta, often called Vietnam's rice bowl, is home to nearly twenty million people and produces much of the country's rice, fruit and seafood. However, this **fertile** region is now facing a growing threat to its water supply, **one** that is created by two connected forces: rising sea levels and prolonged drought. Because the delta lies only a little above sea level, even a small increase in the ocean's height can have dramatic consequences for the communities that live there.
During the dry season, the flow of the Mekong River falls, which allows seawater to push much further inland through the delta's many channels. This process, known as saltwater intrusion, **contaminates** rivers and groundwater that farmers rely on for irrigation and families depend on for drinking and cooking. In recent severe droughts, salt has been detected more than sixty kilometres from the coast, destroying thousands of hectares of rice and forcing many households to buy expensive bottled or delivered water.
The situation is made worse by human activity. Dams built upstream hold back water and sediment, while the excessive pumping of groundwater causes the land itself to sink, so the sea gains ground even faster. As a result, farmers who once depended on predictable seasons now struggle to plan their crops, and many young people have left the countryside to look for work in the cities.
Addressing these challenges will require action on several levels. Provincial authorities should invest in freshwater storage and low-cost systems that purify brackish water, whereas farmers can be encouraged to switch to salt-tolerant rice varieties or to shrimp farming where conditions suit it. Equally important, neighbouring countries along the river must cooperate to manage dams responsibly. Unless such measures are taken promptly, the delta's water crisis is likely to deepen, with consequences that reach far beyond the region itself.

Dams built upstream hold back water and sediment, while the excessive pumping of groundwater causes the land itself to sink, so the sea gains ground even faster. As a result, farmers who once depended on predictable seasons now struggle to plan their crops, and many young people have left the countryside to look for work in the cities.
Addressing these challenges will require action on several levels. Provincial authorities should invest in freshwater storage and low-cost systems that purify brackish water, whereas farmers can be encouraged to switch to salt-tolerant rice varieties or to shrimp farming where conditions suit it. Equally important, neighbouring countries along the river must cooperate to manage dams responsibly. Unless such measures are taken promptly, the delta's water crisis is likely to deepen, with consequences that reach far beyond the region itself.

Dams upstream have no influence on the delta.
Saltwater intrusion only harms fish and shrimp farming.
The delta's water problems may affect people outside the region.

qs.p:
The Mekong Delta, often called Vietnam's rice bowl, is home to nearly twenty million people and produces much of the country's rice, fruit and seafood. However, this **fertile** region is now facing a growing threat to its water supply, **one** that is created by two connected forces: rising sea levels and prolonged drought. Because the delta lies only a little above sea level, even a small increase in the ocean's height can have dramatic consequences for the communities that live there.
During the dry season, the flow of the Mekong River falls, which allows seawater to push much further inland through the delta's many channels. This process, known as saltwater intrusion, **contaminates** rivers and groundwater that farmers rely on for irrigation and families depend on for drinking and cooking. In recent severe droughts, salt has been detected more than sixty kilometres from the coast, destroying thousands of hectares of rice and forcing many households to buy expensive bottled or delivered water.
The situation is made worse by human activity. Dams built upstream hold back water and sediment, while the excessive pumping of groundwater causes the land itself to sink, so the sea gains ground even faster. As a result, farmers who once depended on predictable seasons now struggle to plan their crops, and many young people have left the countryside to look for work in the cities.
Addressing these challenges will require action on several levels. Provincial authorities should invest in freshwater storage and low-cost systems that purify brackish water, whereas farmers can be encouraged to switch to salt-tolerant rice varieties or to shrimp farming where conditions suit it. Equally important, neighbouring countries along the river must cooperate to manage dams responsibly. Unless such measures are taken promptly, the delta's water crisis is likely to deepen, with consequences that reach far beyond the region itself.

The History of Rice Farming in Vietnam

Clean water may seem unlimited when it flows from the tap, but in many parts of the world it is becoming harder to find. Teenagers, **who** will inherit these problems, can start making a difference now through simple choices at home and at school.
One of the easiest places to begin is the bathroom. A shower of ten minutes can use more than a hundred litres of water, so reducing it to five minutes saves a **surprising** amount over a month. Teenagers can also turn off the tap while they brush their teeth or wash their face, which prevents water from running away unused.
Another useful habit is to notice and report waste. If a tap drips or a toilet keeps running, the leak may waste hundreds of litres each week, yet many people never mention it. Students who tell their parents or teachers about such problems can help to fix them **quickly**. In the kitchen, they can wash vegetables in a bowl rather than under running water, and then use that water for the plants.
Finally, teenagers can spread their ideas to others. By making posters for the school noticeboard or sharing short videos online, they can encourage friends and family to follow the same habits. <u>When many people change their behaviour together, the effect on the local water supply becomes much greater than any one person could achieve alone.</u>

a. a. Nam: Is an ethical T-shirt as cheap as a normal one?
b. b. Nam: That makes sense. The more I learn about sweatshops, the more I want to change my habits.
c. c. Nam: Linh, why are you checking the label on that T-shirt so carefully?
d. d. Linh: Not really, but it is as long-lasting as two cheap ones. The more carefully we choose, the less money we waste.
e. e. Linh: I want to know whether it is made from organic cotton and produced by an ethical company.

Hi Gemma,
a. a. Could you bring some clothes you no longer wear and share your tips on shopping for ethical brands?
b. b. I'm writing to invite you to our school's Green Fashion Day, which will be held on 15 May.
c. c. Please let me know by Friday so that I can add your name to the list.
d. d. Many of us used to throw away torn jeans, so this event will help us see them differently.
e. e. Not only will students swap secondhand clothes, but they will also learn how to repair old items for their wardrobe.
Write back soon.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. This habit not only creates mountains of waste but also encourages sweatshops to cut costs.
b. b. Fast fashion has become one of the most serious environmental problems in today's textile industry.
c. c. As a result, consumers buy clothes as quickly as they throw them away.
d. d. In conclusion, we should buy fewer items and choose long-lasting ones instead.
e. e. Hardly has a new trend appeared on social media when cheap copies fill the shelves of big stores.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Therefore, the more consumers support secondhand markets, the less pressure we put on the environment.
b. b. Indeed, a vintage jacket can look as stylish as a brand-new one at a much lower price.
c. c. Many teenagers used to see used clothes as old-fashioned, but social media has changed this view.
d. d. Buying secondhand clothes is becoming a popular way for young people to dress responsibly.
e. e. Not only does this choice save money, but it also reduces the demand for new textiles.

qs.p:
Fast fashion allows consumers to buy trendy clothes at very low prices, but the real price is paid by the environment. Because brands release new collections almost every week, factories must produce huge quantities of clothing, which uses **enormous** amounts of water, energy and raw materials. For example, growing the cotton for a single T-shirt can require thousands of litres of water.
Another serious problem is pollution caused by the textile industry. Many factories dye fabrics with strong chemicals, and in some regions the wastewater is released into rivers without proper treatment. As a result, local communities lose access to clean water, and wildlife suffers as well.
Moreover, most fast fashion items are made from synthetic materials such as polyester, which come from oil. Every time these clothes are washed, **they** release tiny plastic fibres that travel through water systems and eventually reach the ocean. <u>Meanwhile, garments that people throw away after only a few wears often end up in landfills, where they take many years to break down.</u>
Fortunately, consumers can make a difference. By buying fewer items, choosing long-lasting quality, and reading the label carefully, they can encourage companies to adopt **cleaner** methods. Small decisions in a shop may seem unimportant, yet together they can reduce the damage that our love of cheap clothes creates.

qs.p:
For more than a decade, social media encouraged young people to buy more, wear an outfit once and move on to the next trend. Recently, however, a growing number of teenagers and young adults have begun to **challenge** this habit. Instead of filling their cupboards with cheap items, they are saving money for fewer pieces that are well made and designed to last.
One reason for this change is greater awareness of how clothes are produced. Documentaries and online campaigns have exposed sweatshops where employees work long hours for very low wages, and many young consumers say **they** no longer want to support such practices. As a result, they check whether a brand is ethical, read the label for information about materials, and look for certificates that prove fair working conditions.
Another factor is the rising popularity of secondhand shopping. Thrift stores and resale apps, which were once seen as old-fashioned, are now considered smart and creative, because they allow shoppers to find **unique** items while keeping textiles out of landfills. In addition, repairing and restyling clothes has become a fashionable skill that many students proudly share online.
Critics argue that quality products are expensive and therefore unrealistic for people with limited budgets. This is a fair point, yet research suggests that a durable jacket worn for five years often costs less per wear than several cheap ones that fall apart quickly. In conclusion, the shift towards mindful buying shows that fashion and responsibility can go together. Schools, families and brands should support this trend by teaching practical skills such as sewing, promoting honest labelling, and encouraging young people to ask a simple question before every purchase: will I still love this in a year?
