Another factor is the rising popularity of secondhand shopping. Thrift stores and resale apps, which were once seen as old-fashioned, are now considered smart and creative, because they allow shoppers to find **unique** items while keeping textiles out of landfills. In addition, repairing and restyling clothes has become a fashionable skill that many students proudly share online.
Critics argue that quality products are expensive and therefore unrealistic for people with limited budgets. This is a fair point, yet research suggests that a durable jacket worn for five years often costs less per wear than several cheap ones that fall apart quickly. In conclusion, the shift towards mindful buying shows that fashion and responsibility can go together. Schools, families and brands should support this trend by teaching practical skills such as sewing, promoting honest labelling, and encouraging young people to ask a simple question before every purchase: will I still love this in a year?

o: How to Save Money on Cheap Clothes
Why Social Media Is Bad for Fashion
Fewer but Better: Young Shoppers Rethink Fashion
The Return of Old-Fashioned Thrift Stores

qs.p:
Ten years ago, Hai Chau High School in Da Nang was an ordinary school with crowded classrooms, plastic bottles in every corner and little interest in environmental issues. Today, however, it is often described as a model eco-school, and visitors from other provinces regularly travel there to see how it has changed. The **transformation**, according to the principal, began with a single conversation in which a small group of students asked whether they could start an environmental club.
The club quickly became the heart of the school's green movement. Its members, who meet every week, launched a campaign called "Bottle Free Monday", which persuaded most students to bring reusable water bottles instead of buying plastic ones. **They** supported the campaign with colourful posters and a **memorable** slogan, and they also raised funds by selling canvas bags that they had decorated themselves. With the money, they built a rainwater collection system and a vegetable garden, whose produce is used in the school canteen.
What makes the project remarkable is that it has never depended on teachers alone. Student volunteers lead most activities, while teachers act as advisers who offer guidance when it is needed. This approach has given young people a genuine sense of responsibility, and many of them now regard themselves as role models for their families. Several students, for instance, have convinced their parents to sort rubbish at home and to reduce the use of single-use plastic bags at the local market.
The experience of this school suggests that lasting change is possible when students are trusted to take the initiative. Other schools wishing to follow its example should begin by listening to their students, supporting small projects and celebrating every success. If community service becomes part of daily school life rather than an occasional event, awareness will gradually grow into habit, and habit will grow into a greener future for everyone.

Social media has become one of the most effective tools for spreading environmental messages to young people. Teenagers spend several hours online every day, so a short video or an **eye-catching** photo can reach thousands of them within minutes. This is why many environmental groups now design their campaigns specifically for platforms that teenagers already use.
One reason these campaigns work so well is that **they** encourage participation rather than simply giving information. For example, a school club might invite students to post pictures of themselves picking up litter with a special slogan or hashtag. When friends see these posts, they often feel inspired to join in, and the campaign grows quickly. In this way, social media turns ordinary students into volunteers and even role models.
However, online campaigns also have some weaknesses. Some teenagers may click "like" on a post without changing their behaviour, which means that the awareness they gain stays on the screen. In addition, false or **exaggerated** information can spread just as fast as accurate facts, and it can confuse people who are trying to learn.
To make the most of social media, campaigns should connect online activity with real action. A club can, for instance, use a popular post to invite followers to a community service day or a fundraising event. <u>If young people check their sources, share reliable information and then take action offline, they can turn a simple online trend into lasting change in their communities.</u>

qs.p:
Crowded cities are often several degrees hotter than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Concrete, asphalt and glass absorb sunlight during the day and release **it** slowly at night, which makes it difficult for residents to cool down. As global warming **intensifies**, this problem is producing longer and more dangerous heatwaves.
One practical solution is the green roof, which is a layer of soil and plants installed on top of a building. The vegetation shields the roof from direct sunlight, while the water evaporating from its leaves lowers the surrounding temperature. <u>Buildings with green roofs also need less air conditioning, so they save energy and cut greenhouse gas emissions at the same time.</u>
Urban parks offer similar benefits on a larger scale. Tall trees provide shade, and grass and soil absorb rainwater that would otherwise flood the streets. In addition, parks give people places to exercise and relax, which improves their physical and mental well-being.
Of course, creating these spaces is not always easy, because land in city centres is both **scarce** and expensive. Nevertheless, many urban planners believe that combining rooftop gardens, small neighbourhood parks and tree-lined streets is a realistic way to make crowded cities cooler, cleaner and more pleasant to live in.
qs.q: The word "**it**" in paragraph 1 refers to ____.

qs.p:
By 2050, more than two thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities, which makes the design of urban areas one of the most important factors in the fight against climate change. Experts predict that the successful cities of that era will be eco-cities, places where planning, technology and nature work together to keep resources in balance. Although the vision may sound **ambitious**, several cities have already taken their first steps towards it.
One likely change is the way energy is produced and used. Solar panels will cover rooftops and building walls, while smart grids will distribute electricity according to real-time demand, thereby **reducing** waste. Many municipalities hope to become carbon-neutral, meaning that **they** will remove as much carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they release. Transport will also look very different, as electric public vehicles, cycle highways and pedestrian zones replace the traffic jams that currently fill our streets.
Green space will be an essential part of daily life rather than a luxury. Vertical forests, rooftop gardens and restored wetlands will absorb pollution, manage flooding and offer relief during extreme heatwaves, which are expected to become more frequent. Furthermore, local urban farms may supply a significant share of fresh food, shortening the distance between producers and consumers.
Nevertheless, these predictions will come true only if governments, businesses and citizens act now. Policymakers should invest in sustainable development and enforce strict standards for new buildings, while companies must develop cleaner technologies. Ordinary people, particularly the younger generation, can contribute by supporting green policies and adopting environmentally responsible habits. If such cooperation continues, the sustainable city of 2050 will be not a distant dream but a practical reality.

Urban farms will completely replace traditional farming.

qs.p:
By 2050, more than two thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities, which makes the design of urban areas one of the most important factors in the fight against climate change. Experts predict that the successful cities of that era will be eco-cities, places where planning, technology and nature work together to keep resources in balance. Although the vision may sound **ambitious**, several cities have already taken their first steps towards it.
One likely change is the way energy is produced and used. Solar panels will cover rooftops and building walls, while smart grids will distribute electricity according to real-time demand, thereby **reducing** waste. Many municipalities hope to become carbon-neutral, meaning that **they** will remove as much carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they release. Transport will also look very different, as electric public vehicles, cycle highways and pedestrian zones replace the traffic jams that currently fill our streets.
Green space will be an essential part of daily life rather than a luxury. Vertical forests, rooftop gardens and restored wetlands will absorb pollution, manage flooding and offer relief during extreme heatwaves, which are expected to become more frequent. Furthermore, local urban farms may supply a significant share of fresh food, shortening the distance between producers and consumers.
Nevertheless, these predictions will come true only if governments, businesses and citizens act now. Policymakers should invest in sustainable development and enforce strict standards for new buildings, while companies must develop cleaner technologies. Ordinary people, particularly the younger generation, can contribute by supporting green policies and adopting environmentally responsible habits. If such cooperation continues, the sustainable city of 2050 will be not a distant dream but a practical reality.

Dear Mr Tran,
a. a. Many of them say that job opportunities in the nearby industrial zone are the main pull factor.
b. b. Could you recommend a book or an article that explains both kinds of factors?
c. c. I am writing to ask for your advice on my project about why people are moving from rural areas to cities.
d. d. However, I also want to understand the push factors that make farmers leave their land.
e. e. At the moment, more families in my village are leaving, which is a trend that seems to grow every year.
Yours sincerely,

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Nam: Because they want better jobs, which are usually found in big cities.
b. b. Lan: I see. So jobs are the main reason why they move.
c. c. Lan: Why do so many young people leave the countryside these days?

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Indeed, new industrial zones that offer stable wages are attracting thousands of workers every year.
b. b. One reason for this process is population growth, which is increasing the pressure on farmland in many rural areas.
c. c. In conclusion, urbanisation is rising because both rural hardship and urban opportunity are pushing people in the same direction.
d. d. Urbanisation is the process in which a growing share of a country's population settles in towns and cities.
e. e. As a result, young people who cannot find enough work on the land are moving to urban settlements.

Sắp xếp các lượt thoại sau thành một đoạn hội thoại hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. Tuan: Exactly. Farming is becoming harder, so people who want a higher living standard are looking for jobs elsewhere.
b. b. Mai: Is it true that your cousin has moved to Ho Chi Minh City?
c. c. Mai: That makes sense. I think many families will follow the same path.
d. d. Mai: Why did he leave your village? Was farming not enough?
e. e. Tuan: Yes, he is working in an industrial zone which opened near the city last year.

Sắp xếp các câu sau thành một đoạn hoàn chỉnh:
a. a. These two forces work together, which is why the number of urban residents is still rising in many developing countries.
b. b. Migration from rural areas to cities is usually explained by push factors and pull factors.
c. c. Pull factors, on the other hand, are attractions that draw people to cities, for example better schools and higher wages.
d. d. Therefore, any plan that tries to slow urbanisation must deal with both of them.
e. e. Push factors are conditions that make people want to leave their villages, such as poor land, low incomes and natural disasters.

qs.p:
For many young people in Vietnam, the decision to leave their home village is closely linked to work. In rural areas, most jobs depend on farming, (12) ______, so a poor harvest or a fall in crop prices can reduce a family's income overnight. Cities, on the other hand, offer a much wider range of job opportunities, from factory work and construction to office jobs and services, and (13) ______.
This difference in pay is one of the strongest pull factors behind migration. A young worker who earns a stable salary in a city can not only support himself but also send money home, (14) ______. Because of this, (15) ______.

When a neighbour returns to the village with savings and new skills, other young people are encouraged to follow, and the flow of migrants therefore grows year after year. Even so, (16) ______, big cities will continue to attract ambitious young people who hope for a better future.

qs.p:
For generations, the Mekong Delta has been known as the rice bowl of Vietnam, yet in recent decades it has also become one of the country's largest sources of rural-to-urban migrants. Researchers usually explain this trend through two groups of forces: push factors, which make people want to leave their homes, and pull factors, which attract them to a new destination.
Among the push factors, the most serious are linked to the environment and to the farming economy. Rising sea levels, saltwater intrusion and unpredictable floods have damaged orchards and rice fields, leaving many **smallholders** with debts they cannot repay. In addition, farm work has become less profitable because machines have replaced manual labour, which means that fewer people are needed in the fields even when harvests are good.
On the other side, cities such as Ho Chi Minh City and Can Tho exert a **powerful** pull. Their industrial zones employ large numbers of workers, and the wages **they** offer are often two or three times higher than what a labourer can earn at home. Migrants are also drawn by the prospect of better schools for their children, modern hospitals and a generally higher living standard, which they have seen on social media or heard about from relatives who have already moved.
It would be unrealistic, however, to expect this movement to stop, and it would be unwise to treat it only as a problem. A more constructive approach would be to create stable jobs in smaller towns of the Delta, invest in climate-resilient agriculture and improve rural services. If these measures are taken together, people may be able to choose whether to leave rather than feel forced to do so.

attract people to a new destination
force people to abandon their farms

When a province decides to build an industrial zone, its population map can change within just a few years. Before the factories arrive, most residents live in **scattered** villages and earn their living from farming, so the settlements are small and spread out. Once the first companies open, however, the situation begins to change quickly.
The new factories need thousands of workers, and many of **them** come from poorer rural areas in neighbouring provinces. These migrants usually settle close to their workplace, renting rooms in nearby villages or in newly built housing blocks. <u>As a result, a quiet farming community can turn into a crowded town, and its population growth may be much faster than that of the rest of the province.</u>
The effects do not stop at the factory gate. Shops, restaurants, clinics and schools open to serve the newcomers, which creates even more jobs and attracts further migration. Roads and public transport are also improved, so the area becomes better connected to the main city and more **attractive** to investors.
At the same time, regions that lose young workers may face difficulties, because they are left with an older population and fewer people to farm the land. For this reason, local governments need to plan carefully so that growth in one area does not come at the cost of another.

qs.p:
Anyone who has travelled through Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi at six in the evening knows how **exhausting** rush hour can be. Streets that were designed decades ago are now packed with millions of motorbikes and a rapidly growing number of cars, and many commuters spend more than an hour travelling just a few kilometres.
One important reason is the speed of urbanisation. Every year, thousands of people move to these two cities in search of better jobs, and **they** need homes, schools and workplaces that are often far apart. <u>Because the road network has not expanded as quickly as the population, the number of vehicles has far exceeded what the streets can handle.</u>
Another problem is that public transport still carries only a small share of passengers. Bus services are often slow and **unreliable**, while the first metro lines have only just started to operate, so most people feel that owning a private vehicle is the only practical choice. Poor parking, narrow roads and pedestrians crossing at unsafe places make the situation worse.
Experts believe that the congestion will continue unless the cities invest in better public transport and smarter planning. They also suggest that residents could help by using carpools, adjusting working hours or choosing buses and metro trains whenever possible.

qs.p:
For decades, city planners believed that the best way to fight traffic jams was to build more roads. However, experience has shown that wider highways often attract even more vehicles, so the congestion soon returns. As a result, many cities around the world have turned to more **innovative** strategies, notably smart traffic signals and congestion charges.
Smart signals use sensors and cameras to monitor the flow of vehicles in real time and adjust the timing of traffic lights accordingly. In Los Angeles, for example, a computer-controlled system linked thousands of intersections, which reduced average travel times and cut the number of **unnecessary** stops. Since vehicles that keep moving burn less fuel, the technology has also helped to lower emissions, a benefit that residents can feel as well as measure.
A different approach is to charge drivers for entering the busiest areas. London introduced its congestion charge in 2003, and Singapore had developed an electronic road pricing system even earlier. **Both** cities reported a noticeable fall in traffic in their centres, and the money collected was invested in buses, trains and cycling lanes. Critics argue that such charges place a heavier burden on low-income drivers, which is why successful schemes usually offer discounts and, above all, reliable alternatives.
These examples suggest that no single solution is enough on its own. Cities facing severe congestion should combine intelligent technology with fair pricing and, most importantly, high-quality public transport that persuades commuters to leave their cars at home. By doing so, they can create streets that are not only faster but also safer, cleaner and more pleasant for pedestrians and drivers alike.

qs.p:
Over the past three decades, skyscrapers have transformed the skylines of cities from Shanghai to Dubai, and Vietnam's own major cities are following the same path. Developers argue that building upwards is the only sensible answer to rising land prices and growing populations, since a single high-rise can **accommodate** thousands of people on a small piece of land. In theory, this approach should reduce pressure on the suburbs and protect farmland from being swallowed up by expanding cities.
In practice, however, the benefits of vertical growth have not been shared equally. Most new towers are designed as luxury apartments or offices, because these generate the highest profits for investors, and ordinary workers therefore find themselves **excluded** from the very neighbourhoods in which they are employed. Prices have risen so sharply that a young couple on an average salary may need to save for decades before they can even afford the deposit for a mortgage, while those who rent face increases that leave little money for food or transport.
The consequences extend well beyond individual households. When teachers, nurses and shop assistants cannot afford to live near their workplaces, **they** are forced to commute long distances, which worsens traffic and weakens community life. Meanwhile, some of the most expensive apartments remain empty for years because their owners regard them as investments rather than homes, a situation that many residents find deeply unfair.
To address this imbalance, city authorities should require developers to reserve a fixed share of every new project for affordable housing, and they should offer tax benefits to those who comply. Public land could also be used to build good-quality rental flats for low-income families. Without such measures, the cities that celebrate their impressive towers may discover that they have lost the people who keep them running.

Young couples on average salaries can easily afford a mortgage deposit.
Some expensive apartments stay empty because owners see them as investments.
Developers are currently required to reserve part of each project for affordable housing.

qs.p:
Over the past three decades, skyscrapers have transformed the skylines of cities from Shanghai to Dubai, and Vietnam's own major cities are following the same path. Developers argue that building upwards is the only sensible answer to rising land prices and growing populations, since a single high-rise can **accommodate** thousands of people on a small piece of land. In theory, this approach should reduce pressure on the suburbs and protect farmland from being swallowed up by expanding cities.
In practice, however, the benefits of vertical growth have not been shared equally. Most new towers are designed as luxury apartments or offices, because these generate the highest profits for investors, and ordinary workers therefore find themselves **excluded** from the very neighbourhoods in which they are employed. Prices have risen so sharply that a young couple on an average salary may need to save for decades before they can even afford the deposit for a mortgage, while those who rent face increases that leave little money for food or transport.
The consequences extend well beyond individual households. When teachers, nurses and shop assistants cannot afford to live near their workplaces, **they** are forced to commute long distances, which worsens traffic and weakens community life. Meanwhile, some of the most expensive apartments remain empty for years because their owners regard them as investments rather than homes, a situation that many residents find deeply unfair.
To address this imbalance, city authorities should require developers to reserve a fixed share of every new project for affordable housing, and they should offer tax benefits to those who comply. Public land could also be used to build good-quality rental flats for low-income families. Without such measures, the cities that celebrate their impressive towers may discover that they have lost the people who keep them running.

Renting is always a better option than buying a home.

For millions of people in crowded cities, a small apartment of only 25 or 30 square metres is the only affordable choice. Although this may sound uncomfortable, many residents have learned **clever** ways to turn a limited space into a pleasant home. Their experience shows that good planning matters more than size.
One of the most common strategies is to use the walls and ceiling, which are often **ignored**. <u>People fix shelves high above the door, hang hooks for bags and tools, and build beds on raised platforms so that the area underneath can be used as a desk or a wardrobe.</u> Furniture that has more than one purpose is also popular, because a table that folds away can save a surprising amount of room.
Keeping a small home tidy requires good habits as well. Many residents follow the rule that every new object must replace an old one, so **they** regularly give away clothes or books they no longer need. This habit prevents clutter from building up, and it also helps them spend less money on things they do not really want.
Finally, tiny-flat dwellers often treat the neighbourhood as an extension of their home. They meet friends in cafés, exercise in nearby parks and use shared libraries or laundry rooms, which means that they do not need a large living room. In this way, they enjoy a comfortable life even though their private space is small.

qs.p:
Megacities such as Delhi, Jakarta and Beijing are home to millions of people, and many of **them** live with air that regularly **exceeds** safe limits. The pollution comes mainly from vehicle emissions, coal-burning power stations and construction dust, all of which release tiny particles that hang in the air for days. On windless winter mornings, these particles combine with fog to form thick smog, which can reduce visibility and make everyday life uncomfortable.
Children are particularly **vulnerable** to this danger because their lungs are still developing and they breathe faster than adults do. Doctors have found that those who grow up in heavily polluted areas are more likely to suffer from asthma, frequent coughs and chest infections. Some studies even suggest that long-term exposure may slow the growth of their lungs, which could affect their health for the rest of their lives.
The problem is made worse by the fact that many schools and playgrounds are located beside busy roads. <u>Pupils who walk or cycle to school may inhale large amounts of exhaust fumes without realising it, while those who stay indoors are not always protected either.</u> As a result, some schools have started to cancel outdoor sports lessons on days when the air quality is poor.
Fortunately, governments can take action to protect young people. Cleaner public transport, stricter limits on factory emissions and green belts around schools have all produced encouraging results in several cities. Parents, too, can help by checking daily air quality reports and choosing quieter, less congested routes for their children.
qs.q: The word "**them**" in paragraph 1 refers to ____.

qs.p:
Rivers and canals once played a central role in the life of many cities, providing drinking water, transport and space for trade. Today, however, a considerable number of these waterways have been reduced to foul-smelling channels **clogged** with rubbish. Plastic bags, bottles and food packaging are thrown into them every day, and when heavy rain falls, the accumulated waste blocks drains and causes serious flooding in the surrounding streets.
Equally alarming is the problem of sewage. In fast-growing cities, the infrastructure for treating waste water has often failed to keep pace with the rapid increase in population, so that untreated household and industrial discharge flows directly into rivers. This not only contaminates the water with harmful bacteria and chemicals but also deprives fish and plants of the oxygen **they** need to survive. Consequently, once-**thriving** ecosystems have collapsed, and communities that depend on fishing have lost their livelihoods.
The consequences extend well beyond the water itself. Plastic breaks down into microscopic fragments that enter the food chain, eventually reaching the dinner tables of the very people who discarded it. Meanwhile, stagnant water becomes a breeding ground for mosquitoes, which increases the risk of diseases such as dengue fever. Residents living along polluted canals frequently complain of unbearable odours and skin problems, yet many cannot afford to move elsewhere.
Solving this crisis demands coordinated action rather than isolated efforts. Authorities should invest in modern treatment plants, enforce penalties on factories that illegally release waste, and expand reliable collection systems so that rubbish never reaches the water. At the same time, citizens must reduce their use of single-use plastics and take part in recycling programmes. Only when responsibility is shared between government, business and ordinary residents can urban rivers be restored to health.

Consequently, once-**thriving** ecosystems have collapsed, and communities that depend on fishing have lost their livelihoods.
The consequences extend well beyond the water itself. Plastic breaks down into microscopic fragments that enter the food chain, eventually reaching the dinner tables of the very people who discarded it. Meanwhile, stagnant water becomes a breeding ground for mosquitoes, which increases the risk of diseases such as dengue fever. Residents living along polluted canals frequently complain of unbearable odours and skin problems, yet many cannot afford to move elsewhere.
Solving this crisis demands coordinated action rather than isolated efforts. Authorities should invest in modern treatment plants, enforce penalties on factories that illegally release waste, and expand reliable collection systems so that rubbish never reaches the water. At the same time, citizens must reduce their use of single-use plastics and take part in recycling programmes. Only when responsibility is shared between government, business and ordinary residents can urban rivers be restored to health.

qs.p:
When people think of crowded modern cities, **they** rarely imagine places where nature seems to be winning. Yet Singapore, one of the most densely populated countries in the world, has earned the nickname "the City in a Garden" by **weaving** plants into almost every part of its urban landscape. Its planners require new buildings to replace the greenery they remove, which has led to towering vertical gardens, planted rooftops and sky bridges covered in vines. These features not only beautify the skyline but also cool the streets and provide shelter for birds and insects, thereby protecting local biodiversity.
Copenhagen has taken a different path, focusing on how its residents move and what energy they consume. More than half of its inhabitants cycle to work or school every day, a habit made possible by an **extensive** network of safe, separated bike lanes that the city has expanded for decades. Meanwhile, the Danish capital has invested heavily in wind power and district heating, an approach that has significantly reduced its carbon footprint. Its ambitious goal of becoming carbon neutral demonstrates how political determination can transform an entire urban economy.
Although the two cities differ in climate, size and culture, their success rests on a few shared principles. Both governments have treated sustainability as a long-term investment rather than a temporary campaign, and they have encouraged ordinary citizens to take part through incentives, education and public consultation. Furthermore, each city has recognised that green design must be integrated into urban planning from the beginning, instead of being added afterwards as decoration.
For rapidly growing cities elsewhere, including those in Southeast Asia, these examples offer practical guidance. Authorities should set clear environmental targets, prioritise public transport and cycling, and require energy-efficient construction in all new developments. If they combine strong regulation with community involvement, even the busiest cities can become healthier and more liveable places for future generations.

In many large cities, people believe that growing vegetables is impossible because there is no land available. However, a growing number of residents are **proving** otherwise by turning balconies, walls and rooftops into small farms. All they need is a few containers, some good soil and a place that receives enough sunlight. Even a narrow balcony can produce herbs, tomatoes and salad leaves for a family.
Vertical gardens are particularly popular in **crowded** neighbourhoods, since they use wall space instead of the ground. <u>Plants are placed in stacked pots or hanging bags, and a simple pipe system waters them from the top.</u> This method saves both space and water, which makes it ideal for apartment buildings. Some cities have even covered the outside walls of public buildings with edible plants.
Rooftop farms are usually larger and sometimes managed by communities or schools. Neighbours share the work and divide the harvest, and in the process **they** get to know one another better. Rooftop plants also keep the building cooler, so the owners spend less on air conditioning.
Urban farming offers several clear benefits. Fresh vegetables travel only a few metres to the kitchen, which means they stay tasty and produce less pollution than food transported from distant farms. In addition, many people find that caring for plants helps them relax after a stressful day. For these reasons, urban farming is likely to become an even more common part of city life in the future.

qs.p:
Modern cities are becoming smarter because thousands of small sensors are now installed in pipes, streetlights and roads. These devices constantly collect information, which is sent to a central system where powerful software analyses **it**. As a result, city managers can make decisions based on evidence rather than guesswork.
Water management is a good example. Sensors placed inside underground pipes can **detect** sudden changes in pressure, which usually means that water is leaking. Because engineers are alerted immediately, they can repair the damage before large amounts of clean water are wasted. Some cities have reduced their water loss by almost a quarter in this way.
Street lighting and traffic have also been improved. Smart lamps measure how many people or vehicles are nearby and automatically become brighter or dimmer, which saves electricity and lowers the city's costs. Meanwhile, traffic sensors count cars at every junction, and big data programs use this information to adjust traffic lights so that vehicles move more **smoothly** during rush hour.
Despite these benefits, building such systems is expensive, and they must be protected against hackers. <u>Nevertheless, many experts believe that the savings in money, energy and time will gradually outweigh the initial investment, making cities more efficient and more pleasant places to live.</u>
qs.q: The word "**it**" in paragraph 1 refers to ____.

qs.p:
Surveillance cameras equipped with facial recognition software have become a familiar sight in airports, railway stations and shopping streets across the world. Supporters argue that the technology makes public places safer, since it can identify wanted criminals within seconds and help the police find missing children or elderly people who have **wandered** away from home. In crowded cities, where officers cannot possibly monitor every corner, such automated systems appear to offer an efficient solution.
Nevertheless, critics warn that the same technology poses serious threats to personal privacy. When cameras record the faces of millions of innocent citizens every day, **they** create enormous databases that could be **misused** or stolen by hackers. Furthermore, people who know they are constantly being watched may feel less free to attend protests or express their opinions, which could weaken democratic life.
Another concern is accuracy. Several studies have shown that some programs make more mistakes when identifying women and people with darker skin, which means that innocent individuals might be wrongly stopped or even arrested. Because these errors are rarely visible to the public, they are difficult to challenge, and the companies that develop the software are not always required to explain how it works.
In view of these arguments, a balanced approach is clearly necessary. Governments should introduce strict laws that limit where and why facial recognition may be used, require independent testing of the software, and oblige authorities to delete data that is no longer needed. In addition, citizens ought to be informed about where cameras are installed and be given a simple way to complain about abuse. Only with such safeguards can cities enjoy the security benefits of this technology without sacrificing the rights that make urban life worth protecting.

qs.p:
It is a **striking** fact that in many countries, a small number of large cities generate far more than half of the national output, even though they occupy only a tiny fraction of the land. This imbalance is not accidental. Cities bring together huge numbers of workers, companies and customers in a limited space, which allows business to be done faster and more cheaply than in **scattered** rural areas.
One key reason is what economists call the benefits of concentration. When firms in the same industry locate close to one another, they can share suppliers, recruit from the same pool of skilled workers and learn from their competitors. Moreover, a large local market means that even highly specialised services, such as financial consulting or software design, can find enough customers to survive. These advantages explain why ambitious entrepreneurs, who might struggle in a small town, so often choose to start their businesses in the city.
[I] Cities also act as magnets for talent. Universities, hospitals and international companies are usually located there, and **they** offer wages that are considerably higher than those in the countryside. [II] Consequently, millions of people migrate every year in search of better employment, which in turn enlarges the workforce and attracts even more investment. [III] A rising cost of living and a widening income gap between professionals and low-paid workers can leave many residents, especially those in the informal sector, struggling to share in the prosperity that they help to create. [IV]
If cities are to remain engines of growth, governments must ensure that their benefits are shared more fairly. Investing in affordable housing, public transport and vocational training would help low-income residents to take advantage of local opportunities. At the same time, improving roads, internet access and services in smaller towns could spread economic activity more evenly, so that national prosperity does not depend on just a handful of crowded urban centres.

In recent years, the gig economy, in which people earn money from short-term tasks instead of permanent contracts, has grown rapidly in cities around the world. Thanks to smartphone apps, a person can now accept a job within seconds and start earning on the same day. This flexibility is one of the main reasons why so many young people are **attracted** to this kind of work.
Delivery riders are probably the most visible example. **They** travel across busy streets to bring meals and parcels to customers who are too busy to go out, and they are paid for each order they complete. Although some riders can earn a **decent** income during peak hours, they usually have to pay for their own fuel and insurance, and they receive no paid leave if they fall ill.
Freelancers, such as designers, translators and writers, also belong to this group. They choose their own projects and working hours, which many people find rewarding, but they have to look for new clients constantly, so their monthly earnings may be unstable. Meanwhile, street vendors, who have long been part of the informal sector, are using mobile payments and social media to reach more customers than ever before.
Overall, the gig economy offers opportunities to those who might otherwise find it hard to get a stable job. <u>However, because these workers often lack benefits and legal protection, many experts argue that governments should introduce clearer rules to make this new form of employment fairer and safer.</u>

qs.p:
Choosing between the city and the countryside is not easy, because each lifestyle offers advantages that the other cannot match. City dwellers enjoy remarkable convenience: supermarkets stay open late, public transport connects most districts, and hospitals, cinemas and shopping centres are within easy reach. For many young people, this variety of entertainment and opportunities is exactly what makes urban life exciting.
However, the same environment that provides so much can also be **exhausting**. <u>The constant hustle and bustle, long working hours and crowded streets create a level of stress that many residents find hard to manage.</u> Some people feel they are always rushing, which leaves them little time to rest or to enjoy simple pleasures.
Life in the countryside, by contrast, is generally slower and quieter. Villagers usually know one another well, and this close relationship means that neighbours help each other during harvests, celebrations or difficult times. On the other hand, services are **limited**, and young people who want better jobs or education often have to move away.
Interestingly, loneliness is not exclusive to either place. Although the city is full of people, many of **them** hardly speak to anyone outside work, so they may feel isolated in the crowd. Meanwhile, a person in a remote village may feel lonely simply because few people of their age live nearby. Ultimately, the best choice depends on what each person values most.
qs.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 1 as an advantage of city life?

qs.p:
For young people living in big cities, free time has become a surprisingly **complicated** resource. Between long commutes, **demanding** studies and part-time jobs, they often have only a few hours each week to relax, and many of them spend a large share of that time on their phones. Scrolling through short videos or chatting in online groups is cheap, convenient and available at any moment, which explains why it has become the default form of entertainment.
Social media, however, does more than fill empty minutes; it also shapes how young urbanites choose to socialise offline. A cafe becomes popular because it looks good in photographs, and a concert feels worth attending partly because friends will see the pictures. Some sociologists argue that **this** habit turns experiences into content, so people may focus on presenting their lives rather than enjoying them.
Nevertheless, it would be unfair to describe digital habits as entirely harmful. Online networks help newcomers who have just moved to a city to find friends with similar interests, and they make it easy to organise events such as running clubs, language meetings or volunteer projects. In these cases, technology actually reduces loneliness and encourages face-to-face contact, which is precisely what many city residents lack.
The challenge, therefore, is not to abandon social networks but to use them wisely. Young people could set daily limits on screen time, and they might reserve at least one evening a week for activities without phones, such as sport, cooking or visiting a neighbour. Cities and schools can support this balance by providing affordable public spaces, including parks, libraries and community centres, where people can meet naturally. If young urbanites combine the convenience of the digital world with genuine human contact, their free time will become a source of energy rather than distraction.

Scrolling through short videos or chatting in online groups is cheap, convenient and available at any moment, which explains why it has become the default form of entertainment.
Social media, however, does more than fill empty minutes; it also shapes how young urbanites choose to socialise offline. A cafe becomes popular because it looks good in photographs, and a concert feels worth attending partly because friends will see the pictures. Some sociologists argue that **this** habit turns experiences into content, so people may focus on presenting their lives rather than enjoying them.
Nevertheless, it would be unfair to describe digital habits as entirely harmful. Online networks help newcomers who have just moved to a city to find friends with similar interests, and they make it easy to organise events such as running clubs, language meetings or volunteer projects. In these cases, technology actually reduces loneliness and encourages face-to-face contact, which is precisely what many city residents lack.
The challenge, therefore, is not to abandon social networks but to use them wisely. Young people could set daily limits on screen time, and they might reserve at least one evening a week for activities without phones, such as sport, cooking or visiting a neighbour. Cities and schools can support this balance by providing affordable public spaces, including parks, libraries and community centres, where people can meet naturally. If young urbanites combine the convenience of the digital world with genuine human contact, their free time will become a source of energy rather than distraction.

qs.p:
It is no coincidence that the most respected schools, universities and hospitals in a country are usually found in its largest cities. The main reason is **concentration**: a big city gathers a large population in a small area, which creates the demand needed to support expensive, specialised institutions. A hospital that treats rare diseases, for example, needs thousands of potential patients nearby to justify its costly equipment, and a city can provide them.
Money and talent also play an important role. Cities generate more tax revenue and private investment than rural areas, so governments and businesses can afford to build modern facilities and pay high salaries. These conditions attract skilled teachers, researchers and doctors, who often prefer to work where they can collaborate with colleagues and continue **their** professional development. In turn, their reputation draws **ambitious** students and patients from other regions, which strengthens the institutions even further.
Unfortunately, this cycle has a less positive side. Families from the countryside frequently migrate to cities in search of better opportunities, and this puts great pressure on classrooms and hospital wards. Enrolment at popular schools may exceed capacity, while patients sometimes wait many hours for treatment. Meanwhile, smaller towns lose their most talented professionals, and the gap in literacy rates and life expectancy between regions may widen.
To address this imbalance, policymakers should invest more in education and health care outside major cities. Practical measures could include offering scholarships to students who agree to work in rural areas, building regional hospitals with modern equipment, and using digital technology to connect local staff with city specialists. If such steps are taken, the benefits of urban development can be shared more fairly across the whole country.

In many cities, residents who live in the centre enjoy a wide range of public services within a short walking distance. Schools, hospitals, libraries and parks are close at hand, and public transport arrives frequently. People in **outlying** districts, however, often have a very different experience of the same city.
One major difference is the number and quality of facilities. Outlying districts usually grow quickly as families look for **cheaper** housing, but the government does not always build new schools and clinics fast enough to keep up. As a result, children may have to travel long distances to attend class, and patients may wait a long time to see a doctor.
Another problem is transport, **which** affects almost every other service. When buses are rare or roads are poorly maintained, even a well-equipped hospital in the centre is difficult for distant residents to reach. This is why many people in these areas delay medical visits until their conditions become serious, and why some students miss lessons during the rainy season.
Fortunately, there are ways to reduce this gap. <u>Local authorities can plan new neighbourhoods together with schools, clinics and bus routes, so that services are ready before residents arrive.</u> They can also use mobile health units and online classes to reach families who live far from the centre. If these solutions are applied consistently, the whole city will become fairer and more comfortable for everyone.

qs.p:
In many Asian cities, the old quarter is both the most charming and the most **vulnerable** area. Its narrow streets, shop-houses and busy traditional markets reflect centuries of trade and daily life, which is why visitors and residents alike value them so highly. Nevertheless, these districts are often crowded, noisy and short of modern facilities, so city authorities are tempted to clear them for new developments.
Redevelopment, however, does not have to mean **destruction**. In some cities, officials have chosen to upgrade the drainage, electricity and fire safety of old houses instead of replacing them. Residents who stayed were able to keep their homes and their shops, and the streets kept the atmosphere that had made them famous. <u>Such renovation projects usually cost more time and patience, but they protect something that no new tower can offer.</u>
Traditional markets deserve the same attention. **They** are not only places to buy fresh food at fair prices; they are also social spaces where neighbours meet and where skills and recipes are passed down. When a market is moved to a distant shopping centre, the customers it served often stop visiting and small traders lose their income. A better approach is to improve hygiene and organisation within the existing market while limiting traffic around it.
Ultimately, a modern city should be judged not only by its skyscrapers but also by how well it respects the places that gave it character. By combining careful preservation with sensible improvements, urban planners can build a future that people feel proud to belong to.

qs.p:
By 2050, demographers expect nearly seven out of ten people on Earth to live in urban areas, and the number of megacities, those with more than ten million **inhabitants**, is likely to rise sharply, particularly in Asia and Africa. Cities such as Lagos, Dhaka and Ho Chi Minh City may grow so quickly that their boundaries become difficult to define. As a result, the line between city and countryside could almost disappear.
One probable consequence is the continued spread of urban sprawl, as people move to the outskirts in search of cheaper land. **This** pattern, however, brings long commutes, higher costs for infrastructure and the loss of farmland. To avoid these problems, many experts predict that successful cities will grow upwards and inwards instead, **concentrating** homes, offices and shops around public transport hubs. Residents may spend most of their daily lives within a short walk of where they live, which would reduce both travel time and pollution.
Geography will also shape where people settle. Coastal megacities face rising sea levels, so some governments may be forced to build protective barriers or even relocate entire districts inland. Meanwhile, smaller cities with milder climates and lower living costs could attract workers who are able to do their jobs remotely, easing pressure on the largest centres.
Given these trends, planning must start today rather than tomorrow. Governments should prepare a long-term master plan that sets aside land for housing, green space and transport before prices become unaffordable. They should also protect historic landmarks and neighbourhoods, since a city that loses its heritage risks losing its identity. If these measures are combined with fair and open decision-making, the megacities of 2050 could be places that are not only larger but also more liveable than those of today.

Cities such as Lagos, Dhaka and Ho Chi Minh City may grow so quickly that their boundaries become difficult to define. As a result, the line between city and countryside could almost disappear.
One probable consequence is the continued spread of urban sprawl, as people move to the outskirts in search of cheaper land. **This** pattern, however, brings long commutes, higher costs for infrastructure and the loss of farmland. To avoid these problems, many experts predict that successful cities will grow upwards and inwards instead, **concentrating** homes, offices and shops around public transport hubs. Residents may spend most of their daily lives within a short walk of where they live, which would reduce both travel time and pollution.
Geography will also shape where people settle. Coastal megacities face rising sea levels, so some governments may be forced to build protective barriers or even relocate entire districts inland. Meanwhile, smaller cities with milder climates and lower living costs could attract workers who are able to do their jobs remotely, easing pressure on the largest centres.
Given these trends, planning must start today rather than tomorrow. Governments should prepare a long-term master plan that sets aside land for housing, green space and transport before prices become unaffordable. They should also protect historic landmarks and neighbourhoods, since a city that loses its heritage risks losing its identity. If these measures are combined with fair and open decision-making, the megacities of 2050 could be places that are not only larger but also more liveable than those of today.

qs.p:
Half a century ago, the job market in most countries was dominated by agriculture and manufacturing. A typical worker expected to join a company in his or her twenties, learn one set of skills and stay in the same line of work until retirement. In many families, a single breadwinner, usually the father, earned enough to support everyone, and blue-collar jobs in factories, mines and construction offered **stable** wages even to those with little formal education.
Since then, several forces have **reshaped** the workforce. Globalisation moved much of the manufacturing industry to countries where labour was cheaper, while automation allowed machines to perform tasks that once required dozens of people. As a result, the service sector, which includes healthcare, finance, education and tourism, has grown dramatically, and white-collar positions now account for a far larger share of employment than **they** did in the past.
The nature of employment itself has also altered. Women have entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers, so that households with two incomes are now common. Meanwhile, the idea of a lifelong job has largely disappeared, replaced by short contracts, freelance projects and frequent career changes. Although this flexibility gives people more freedom, it also brings insecurity, since workers can no longer rely on a single employer to guarantee their future.
Given these trends, young people entering the job market today should be prepared to keep learning throughout their lives. Schools, therefore, ought to teach adaptability and critical thinking as well as technical knowledge, and governments should support retraining programmes for those whose occupations are disappearing. Only by combining individual effort with institutional support can societies ensure that the next fifty years of change create opportunities rather than inequality.

The terms blue-collar and white-collar are often used to divide the world of work into two broad groups. Blue-collar workers, such as builders, mechanics and factory operators, usually perform physical or technical tasks, while white-collar workers, such as accountants, managers and administrators, mostly work in offices and handle information. Although the division is not perfect, it helps us understand how daily life can differ between the two.
A blue-collar worker often starts early and spends the day on a construction site, in a workshop or on a production line. The work can be tiring and sometimes dangerous, but it also offers a sense of achievement, because the results are visible at the end of each day. In contrast, an office employee typically sits at a desk, attends meetings and communicates by email, which is less physically **demanding** but can cause stress and long hours in front of a screen.
Pay and job security vary in both groups. Skilled tradespeople, for instance, may earn more than some office staff, and **they** are always needed because buildings, machines and cars must be repaired. <u>White-collar jobs, however, often provide more opportunities for promotion and are usually linked to higher levels of education, which is why many parents encourage their children to pursue them.</u>
Looking ahead, the boundary between the two categories is becoming less **clear**. Modern technicians use computers to operate machines, and many office workers learn practical skills as well. Consequently, the best choice for a young person is not the type of collar but the career that suits their abilities and interests.
